title: What’s new with Google Data Cloud
raw_text: October 19 - October 23 BigQuery introduces column aliases in GoogleSQL and cross-region table copy GA GoogleSQL in BigQuery now supports column aliases in SELECT and WHERE clauses (GA opt-in), avoiding nested subqueries and simplifying migrations from Snowflake and Teradata. Cross-region table copying is also now generally available to streamline regional data replication and disaster recovery. Review the BigQuery release notes . Conversational analytics in BigQuery expands to Canada and adds CSV/PDF export Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now available in Montréal ( northamerica-northeast1 ) and Toronto ( northamerica-northeast2 ) to support Canadian data residency requirements. You can also now export agent responses — including text, tables, charts, and citations — directly to CSV or PDF (GA). Learn more about conversational analytics in BigQuery . AlloyDB Omni 18.4.0 is now GA with Advanced Query Insights and external KMS support AlloyDB Omni 18.4.0 brings PostgreSQL 18.4 to self-hosted and multi-cloud environments, adding the google_insights_v2 extension for granular query execution and wait-event diagnostics. It also adds Thales CipherTrust Manager support for Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) alongside HashiCorp Vault. Explore the AlloyDB Omni release notes . Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL adds managed connection pooling and Private Service Connect defaults Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now supports enabling built-in managed connection pooling on existing Private Service Connect (PSC) instances to scale high-concurrency workloads. PSC is also now the default private IP option for new Cloud SQL instances in new projects to simplify cross-project networking. Review Cloud SQL updates . Customer momentum: Unico prevents over $5B in fraud on Google's Agentic Data Cloud Digital identity platform Unico migrated from Databricks Spark/Scala clusters to BigQuery and Spanner at the core of its data architecture. Unifying real-time transaction streams with petabyte-scale analytics enabled low-latency identity verification that has prevented over $5 billion in fraud. Read the Unico case study . Developer guide: Getting started with Looker Data Apps Following the debut of Looker Data Apps in preview, a new walkthrough on the Google Developer Community shares practical patterns for building prompt-driven applications inside Looker. Read the guide on the Google Developer Community . October 12 - October 16 Looker Data Apps are now in Preview to build and host interactive, agent-generated applications natively inside Looker Generated using natural language prompts, the Antigravity CLI, or Claude Code, these interactive web applications, natively hosted inside Looker, transform business reporting into operational systems of action. Users can test scenarios, adjust parameters, and trigger workflows in downstream platforms while inheriting LookML semantic modeling, row-level security, and access controls with no runtime LLM token costs. Read the announcement blog . Build end-to-end data science pipelines with the Data Agent Kit Following the general availability of the Data Agent Kit , a new end-to-end walkthrough demonstrates how data teams can build, test, and schedule machine learning pipelines directly from their preferred code editors. Explore the walkthrough and codelab . Manage dashboard agents as code to bring CI/CD and version control to LookML dashboards Data teams can now declare agent parameters, configurations, and prompt instructions alongside dashboard files in code. This integration enables standard developer workflows for conversational BI, including Git version control, peer review, branching, and automated CI/CD validation before agent modifications reach production end users. Read the technical guide on the Google Developer Community . Simplify AI search with native AlloyDB hybrid search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion AlloyDB for PostgreSQL simplifies hybrid search architectures by combining vector similarity search and keyword BM25 retrieval within a unified database engine. Using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), developers can merge lexical scoring and semantic embeddings into a single ranked result without writing a complex SQL query. This unified approach removes the operational overhead of running and synchronizing external search engines alongside operational databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and search applications. Explore hybrid search in AlloyDB . October 5 - October 9 Data Agent Kit is now generally available to bring Google Data Cloud to any coding agent Data Agent Kit provides a free collection of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and Google-authored agent skills that connect more than 15 Google Data Cloud services directly to coding agents across VS Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. This release expands support for developers and data practitioners to inspect schemas, author queries, and build end-to-end data pipelines in natural language directly from their IDE or CLI. Read the announcement blog . Spanner Omni is now generally available for deploy-anywhere, multi-model workloads Spanner Omni brings Spanner's distributed SQL, graph, vector, and key-value capabilities to any environment, including on-premises data centers, other public clouds via Kubernetes or VMs, and local developer laptops. Organizations can build and run multi-model applications with consistent APIs and query engines across hybrid and multi-cloud footprints while seamlessly scaling to managed Spanner on Google Cloud. Read the launch blog and explore how Spanner also removed cumulative mutation limits for DML transactions . AlloyDB delivers PostgreSQL for agents and native BM25 hybrid search We announced PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB , introducing an agentic database architecture engineered for real-time data access at agent scale with workload isolation. In addition, native BM25 ranking is now in Preview for AlloyDB and Cloud SQL , allowing developers to combine keyword search and vector embeddings directly in PostgreSQL without maintaining an external search engine. For hybrid deployments, the AlloyDB Omni RPM Orchestrator is now generally available , and you can dive deeper in our new Build AI apps and agents with AlloyDB eBook . Lakehouse runtime catalog adds regional endpoints across 22 regions and GA support for flexible column names Lakehouse runtime catalog regional endpoints are now live across 22 Google Cloud regions across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East, supporting both the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint and the Apache Hive catalog endpoint to help customers meet strict data residency and sovereignty requirements. In addition, flexible column names for Apache Iceberg tables are now generally available by default across Iceberg external tables and managed tables, enabling seamless querying of columns containing spaces, hyphens, and Unicode characters. We also announced the Preview of cross-cloud caching and connections for the borderless Lakehouse . Unlock predictive and agent-ready insights with BigQuery augmented analytics TVFs, TabFM, and identity columns BigQuery introduced augmented analytics table-valued functions (TVFs) : six built-in functions that automate metric diagnostics, trend analysis, and pattern discovery directly where your data lives and integrate as skills for AI agents. We also introduced TabFM in BigQuery to bring tabular foundation model capabilities to predictive analytics, alongside BigQuery identity columns to automatically generate sequential surrogate keys and simplify data warehouse pipelines. Dataflow adds Pause/Resume and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU support for large-scale AI workloads New Dataflow capabilities make it easier to run high-throughput streaming and batch AI pipelines at scale, including Pause/Resume job controls and support for NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. And for teams running Apache Spark workloads, learn how to mitigate compute stockouts and maximize availability using flexible VMs . Unlock up to 3x higher QPS and microsecond latency with Memorystore for Valkey 9.1 Memorystore for Valkey 9.1 is now available, delivering up to 3x higher queries per second (QPS) and microsecond-level caching latencies to accelerate high-throughput applications and real-time AI agent state management. Read the blog . Customer momentum across Google Data Cloud — Yahoo, PayPal, Surescripts, Airwallex, and Lucius AI Organizations across industries are scaling their data and AI foundations on Google Data Cloud. Yahoo uses flexible VMs in Managed Service for Apache Spark to reduce provisioning failures by 85%, while PayPal migrated mission-critical analytics workloads to Managed Service for Apache Spark to scale and reduce operational overhead. On the database front, Surescripts migrated 30.5 billion annual healthcare transactions to AlloyDB with 99.998% uptime, Airwallex manages more than 5,000 databases with 99.99% availability on Cloud SQL with a team of four DBAs, and Lucius AI runs a 210,000-tender global platform on AlloyDB and MCP with 47x faster ScaNN vector search. September 7 - September 10 Pub/Sub SMTs can now AI Inference your Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models! Pub/Sub AI Inference SMTs allow you to apply inference on an incoming stream of events using models hosted in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The model’s prediction is appended to your event, making it available for downstream processing in your data warehouse (like BigQuery) or operational database (like BigTable). This feature, now generally available, can dramatically simplify or enhance anomaly detection systems you are operating. PostgreSQL Source Connector is now generally available in Managed Service for Apache Kafka! Managed Service for Apache Kafka’s PostgreSQL connector allows customers to capture changes from their PostgreSQL database and ingest them into their Kafka infrastructure with low latency. This source connector is compatible with Cloud SQL for Postgres , AlloyDB, and self-managed PostgreSQL databases. Try this along with our entire portfolio of managed connectors, including MirrorMaker 2.0, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Pub/Sub ! E-mail kafka-hotline@google.com if you have questions or feedback! Pause-on-failure for Dataflow batch jobs is GA Dataflow pause-on-failure enables you to preserve the state of a batch Dataflow job before it fails. By pausing your Dataflow job, you can address issues that are external to the pipeline and resume processing without losing completed work. This helps you better manage resource costs and improve job reliability when you face temporary outages or capacity constraints. The insertAll API is now the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST) The legacy insertAll streaming API is now rebranded as the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST). By dropping the "legacy" label, developers can confidently build long-term HTTP-based streaming workflows. This stateless JSON-over-HTTPS endpoint offers a lightweight alternative to heavy gRPC libraries—ideal for serverless web apps, IoT telemetry, and AI logging. The transition is seamless for existing users, requiring zero code changes and offering 100% backward compatibility. However, the Storage Write API (gRPC) version remains the recommended standard for high-throughput, continuous pipelines. August 31 - September 4 Stateful processing is available in BigQuery continuous queries in Preview Stateful operations significantly expand what’s possible with BigQuery continuous queries. This feature allows users to leverage functions like JOIN s, aggregations, and windowing functions directly in their streaming queries. Now you can calculate metrics over time (for example, a 30-minute average) to power your downstream applications and AI agents with much richer, real-time signals. Try out our feature here and share your feedback with bq-continuous-queries-feedback@google.com! Synthetic data generator tool is available for Managed Service for Kafka You’ve launched your first Kafka cluster. Now what? The next thing to do is to produce some data to the cluster, but that involves modifying a client application somewhere or spinning up a virtual machine. The synthetic data generator tool, now generally available, can start sending mock data to your cluster in 3 clicks, and will get data streaming into your cluster in less than two minutes. The perfect utility for those moments you just want to test your cluster and new features. Try our quickstart today! title: Cloud CISO Perspectives: Introducing new $250,000 tier for Google Cloud VRP (Q&A)
raw_text: Welcome to the second Cloud CISO Perspectives for October 2026. Today, Chris Betz talks with Michael Cote, our vulnerability rewards program lead, about the new tier of our Cloud VRP program and the current state of vulnerability rewards. As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog . If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here . aside_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('title', 'Get vital board insights with Google Cloud'), ('body', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecdad1d90>), ('btn_text', 'Visit the hub'), ('href', 'https://cloud.google.com/solutions/security/board-of-directors?utm_source=cgc-site&utm_medium=et&utm_campaign=FY26-Q2-GLOBAL-GCP39634-email-dl-dgcsm-CISOP-NL-177159&utm_content=-&utm_term=-'), ('image', None)])]> Why we've created a new $250,000 tier for Google Cloud VRP (Q&A) By Chris Betz, CISO, Google Cloud The Google Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) partners with the global security research community to help elevate cloud security for all by encouraging the discovery of critical software vulnerabilities. In an era when automated research has made it more challenging to verify authentic vulnerabilities, we have a critical need to boost high-level, human-led research that can transcend automated-only discovery. Today, we are expanding our top reward tier with a new $250,000 Root-in-Cloud reward , specifically designed to recognize high-impact architectural research. Identifying tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws requires human creativity, intuition, and rigorous systems analysis combined with the power of agentic systems. To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of “roles/owner” or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup. The exploit path can not depend on: Pre-existing access or footholds in the victim project. Leaked, phished, or stolen credentials. User interaction or social engineering. Proof-of-root: Clear, cryptographic validation To make testing safe, clear, and reproducible, without impacting production environments, we have defined technical criteria for validating root-in-cloud access . Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility. Because code execution in Borg has the potential to impact service availability or cross-tenant data, researchers must halt all probing immediately upon achieving any execution in Borg. Escalation, extracting production credentials, and lateral movement are not allowed and will result in researcher disqualification. The Google Cloud VRP panel will analyze the initial entry point, execution context, and attack surface to determine whether full arbitrary tenant or project takeover is achievable from that position, and award the bounty accordingly. This new bounty tier reflects how security research continues to evolve, and the importance of continuing to recognize the most innovative and valuable security research. As part of those efforts, Google Security held its annual Escal8 conference in Singapore last week, and I had the opportunity to discuss the changing landscape with Michael Cote, Google Cloud’s vulnerability reward program lead. The following transcript has been lightly edited. Chris Betz : You are at Escal8 in Singapore announcing the new $250,000 Root-in-Cloud tier for our VRP. Why introduce this tier now, and what kind of research are you hoping to spark? Michael Cote : This is a recognition of how the field of security research has changed over the past year. We value quality submissions from anyone, and we’ve seen that the combination of human creativity and agentic power is much richer than either on its own. While automated scanners generate a high volume of low-impact noise, first-time researchers who pair human intuition with agentic tools are finding, on average, more interesting bugs than novices did two years ago. With the new Root-in-Cloud tier, we want to challenge the community and increasingly reward the complex, high-impact findings — like tenant-isolation bypasses and cross-service logic flaws — that require deep architectural intuition alongside agentic tools, because getting that information is essential to protecting our customers. Chris Betz : Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) recently shared research showing that monthly CVE disclosures have doubled as agentic tools mature. From your seat leading the Cloud VRP, how has automation technology impacted the reports we’ve received? Michael Cote : It has transformed our intake volume, though not in the way many people assume. While the number of valid vulnerability reports submitted to the Google Cloud VRP has remained stable over the last 18 months, the total number of reports has grown tremendously. Automation has helped democratize vulnerability discovery, and the barrier to entry has been rapidly flattening, something even our top researchers noted at Escal8. Because we’re seeing more researchers and more first-timers with interesting bugs, that creates pressure on more experienced researchers to move faster and bring more impactful findings — although their experience continues to be a key differentiator in success. Chris Betz : I’ve been working with the research community for more than 20 years. One of the things I appreciate most is how much the community values making the world more secure. Bounty programs let us recognize this valuable work. How do you see the community changing as we move further into the agentic era? Michael Cote : That shared commitment to making the world more secure is still the heart of this community, which is why the pressure to move faster is something we have to watch closely. As our GTIG colleagues found, the sharpest rise in the number of exploited vulnerabilities comes from n-days, not zero-days . Open source accounts have suggested that threat actors are using LLMs to rapidly turn newly-public vulnerability details into working exploits. When triage teams are already working through a surge in report volume, disclosing an unmitigated vulnerability well ahead of the standard 90-day coordinated disclosure window gives attackers the exact knowledge and time window they need to target customers. With the influx of new submissions, I worry about a growing pressure to rush to publish. Something that concerns me because we’re already seeing early indications of it. Because LLMs lower the barrier to finding bugs in source-available software, researchers worry that waiting to verify risks will allow someone else to be first to publish. Even more concerning, that same competitive pressure can tempt even established security companies to disclose unmitigated vulnerabilities without coordination, and that rush puts our users directly at risk. Project Zero helped establish the industry’s 90-plus-30-day responsible disclosure policy, and autonomous detection and exploitation capabilities make following coordinated disclosure more important than ever. In the long run, rushing to be first works against a security company's own self-interest. Novel discoveries may bring temporary visibility, but customers will ultimately choose not to work with organizations that put them and the broader ecosystem at risk. Chris Betz : When you offer a $250,000 bounty, how do you make sure researchers can validate their findings without putting customer environments or service availability at risk? Michael Cote : High incentives require clear, safe rules of engagement. We never want researchers testing exploits against real customer projects. Instead, we created a deterministic proof-of-root mechanism using a designated service account. Researchers can cryptographically prove unauthorized access against that identity. We’ve also updated our program rules to establish strict boundaries around underlying production infrastructure. If researchers think they are close to a breakthrough but are uncertain where the boundary lies, we encourage them to reach out. We are always more than happy to work with them to ensure they are recognized and rewarded for the value of their research without taking steps that would invalidate the bounty. Chris Betz : What should enterprise CISOs take away from these trends? Especially those who run their own vulnerability management pipelines and partner with external researchers, what advice would you offer for navigating this AI inflection point? Michael Cote : First, prepare your vulnerability triage workflows for agent-generated submissions. To keep valid reports from getting stuck in a backlog, security teams need ways to separate plausible-sounding hallucinations from real security risks. Second, compress your remediation timelines once a vulnerability becomes public. Defensive patching and mitigations have to move faster because autonomous technology compresses the time from disclosure to working exploits. Finally, hold your security partners and vendors to high standards of coordinated disclosure. It’s important that our industry continues to normalize agentic vulnerability research , but we must do so responsibly. Let’s continue to keep user safety at the center of everything we do. For more information on the Google Cloud VRP, including detailed endpoint specifications, JSON payloads, and CLI examples, please check out our rules page . aside_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('title', 'Join the Google Cloud CISO Community'), ('body', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecdad1f90>), ('btn_text', 'Learn more'), ('href', 'https://rsvp.withgoogle.com/events/google-cloud-ciso-community-interest-form-2026?utm_source=cgc-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=FY25-Q1-global-GCP30328-physicalevent-er-dgcsm-parent-CISO-community-2025&utm_content=cisop_&utm_term=-'), ('image', None)])]> In case you missed it Here are the latest updates, products, services, and resources from our security teams so far this month: How Google Does It: Using agents to help find, track, and fix vulnerabilities : Threat actors can now find software flaws faster than ever. title: Querying Databricks Apache Iceberg Tables with the borderless Lakehouse
raw_text:
Enterprise organizations often leverage multiple data platforms, including Databricks, to execute heavy Apache Spark jobs alongside BigQuery to power highly concurrent analytics workloads. Historically, bridging these systems often meant building complex pipelines to copy data between environments. This approach increases storage costs, introduces latency, and fragments security controls. With Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse, you can now query Databricks-managed Apache Iceberg tables straight from BigQuery. This zero-copy approach removes the need to duplicate data: BigQuery reads the same files Databricks writes, and new changes appear after Lakehouse's next scheduled metadata refresh (as often as every 5 minutes). How Lakehouse and Databricks work together Managed Iceberg tables automatically generates Iceberg-compatible metadata alongside native Delta logs. Data engineering teams can store Parquet files once in Google Cloud Storage (GCS) using Databricks. Rather than loading this information into BigQuery, Lakehouse reads the Iceberg metadata directly, applying BigQuery’s vectorized engine directly to open-format files in GCS. Although Google Cloud Storage (GCS) serves as the primary storage layer in the above example, Lakehouse extends this borderless federation directly to external cloud environments like Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage. By pairing the open Apache Iceberg REST Catalog with cross-cloud connections, Lakehouse lets BigQuery query data across clouds without moving it. Each federated catalog lives in a Google Cloud location you choose, ideally the region closest to your data. This lets BigQuery read open-format Parquet files where they live, delivering multi-cloud analytics without replication pipelines. Remote-cloud egress charges still apply, but Cross-Cloud Interconnect (AWS) and Lakehouse caching can reduce them. Beyond simply querying external data, Lakehouse framework establishes true read and write (R/W) interoperability across engines. Because the platform is built on an open Apache Iceberg foundation, data teams can effortlessly execute multi-statement SQL commands directly inside BigQuery. Centralized security and governance Handling access controls across disparate systems can introduce vulnerabilities. Lakehouse addresses this through delegated access. Administrators can configure a BigQuery Cloud Resource Connection tied to a service account that manages IAM rights for GCS buckets. Granting users access to the Lakehouse table entity lets you enforce BigQuery controls including row-level, column-level security, and dynamic data masking on external Iceberg tables while Databricks handles ingestion. Catalog federation and credential vending Previously, connecting these platforms meant manually configuring BigQuery queries to point at static metadata paths. Modern setups leverage the open Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API. Databricks Unity Catalog functions as the central metadata layer, allowing a BigQuery administrator to establish a Lakehouse runtime catalog with a federated connection. When running a query, Lakehouse contacts Unity Catalog for current table state, and short-lived tokens are issued through credential vending to grant BigQuery temporary read access to GCS. Partition pruning BigQuery uses each table's Iceberg metadata to plan the query, then reads only the relevant data files in place. Iceberg's hidden partitioning lets you filter on logical columns, such as timestamps, without knowing the directory layout. Note that Databricks managed Iceberg tables don't support partition transforms; Databricks recommends liquid clustering instead. Filters in a standard WHERE clause let BigQuery use the Iceberg manifests to skip partitions that can't match. Compare partition columns with literal values so pruning can apply. These manifests maintain detailed column-level statistical bounds, enabling BigQuery to bypass irrelevant manifest records and unneeded Parquet files immediately. Consequently, queries scan only necessary byte ranges, accelerating query execution while significantly reducing on-demand slot consumption and storage scan costs. Fast queries with Iceberg metadata and Lakehouse caching Iceberg manifests already identify which data files to read, so BigQuery doesn't need a metadata cache for Iceberg tables. For cross-cloud tables, such as those in Amazon S3, Lakehouse caching (Preview) keeps retrieved data blocks in Google Cloud so repeat queries read them locally. BigQuery reads the Iceberg manifest files directly when it plans each query; there's no metadata caching to enable. This dynamic partition pruning bypasses unneeded files, significantly reducing runtime and bytes scanned. Maintenance and lifecycle management Modern lakehouses demand active upkeep; without routine care, performance degrades into an inefficient repository. Fortunately, both BigQuery and Databricks supply native capabilities to preserve table hygiene and accelerate analytical workloads. Keeping your tables optimized To maintain optimal query performance, active maintenance of your lakehouse storage footprint remains necessary. Trigger regular compaction pipelines via Databricks APIs to merge tiny Parquet files into larger, optimized layouts and use Predictive Optimization. Execute the Databricks VACUUM command to clear unreferenced files outside active snapshots, avoiding extra GCS storage costs. Compaction and the small file problem Frequent write operations, continuous ingestion jobs, and streaming workloads continuously produce thousands of small Parquet files. This fragmentation creates a storage bottleneck that can limit BigQuery’s reading efficiency. Establishing thousands of network connections to GCS and processing metadata footers across numerous tiny files consumes significant compute time, diminishing the performance advantages of vectorized query execution. Running routine compaction within Iceberg resolves these inefficiencies. Databricks manages this automatically using Liquid Clustering which dynamically adjusts file layouts based on access patterns or through native table management utilities. To compact small files manually on Databricks, run OPTIMIZE: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run on Databricks to compact small files
-- On Databricks:
OPTIMIZE customer_events;
-- For Iceberg tables you manage outside Databricks:
CALL my_catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(
table => 'default.customer_events',
strategy => 'binpack',
options => map(
'target-file-size-bytes',
'268435456',
'min-file-size-bytes',
'67108864'
)
);"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecd36c4d0>)])]> Executing this command aggregates scattered file segments into larger, structured blocks typically between 256MB and 512MB that can help improve BigQuery’s scan throughput. The binpack approach operates rapidly by prioritizing total file size balancing, though alternative sorting strategies can organize dataset ordering along specific column keys. Managing orphan files and snapshot retention (VACUUM) Every transactional update, record modification, and table compaction creates fresh snapshots within Iceberg to preserve dataset integrity. Over time, historical Parquet objects detached from active table states become orphaned. Although these legacy files facilitate time-travel analytics, neglecting them can drive up GCS storage charges over time. Data teams can use the Databricks VACUUM operation to scan and purge abandoned storage files. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "ALTER TABLE customer_events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = '7 days');
VACUUM customer_events FULL;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecdcb3510>)])]> Standard configurations apply a mandatory seven-day threshold (deletedFileRetentionDuration) before executing VACUUM routines. Preserving this delay prevents active analytical jobs from encountering missing file errors while keeping historical recovery options available. Scheduling routine VACUUM jobs, or letting predictive optimization run them, removes unreferenced data files and, for tables with Iceberg reads, old Iceberg metadata. That keeps storage costs low and performance high across your lakehouse. Conclusion Connecting Databricks Apache Iceberg datasets to Lakehouse can help you activate your data with BigQuery. By separating processing from underlying storage, embracing open formats, and using standard REST APIs with credential vending, you can run scalable engineering workloads and concurrent analytics without migrating data or sacrificing performance Pairing Databricks Iceberg reads (UniForm) with Lakehouse federation, Lakehouse caching, and regular OPTIMIZE and VACUUM maintenance helps you build an efficient, zero-copy lakehouse. This approach can help lower storage spend, avoids fragile pipeline maintenance, and prepares your data environment for modern analytics and emerging AI workloads. Constructing a unified architecture no longer requires moving data files across platforms. You can begin querying Databricks Iceberg tables by registering them with the Lakehouse runtime catalog today for bi-directional federation. Learn more by reading our documentation to get started.

title: Grounding agents in one context graph connecting semantic models you already trust
raw_text: Picture the scene: Before an executive business review, your VP of Sales asks an AI assistant, "What was net revenue for our top enterprise accounts last quarter?" In seconds, the agent returns a polished chart! Unfortunately, the numbers don't match the finance report. Why? Because the agent counted cancelled orders as revenue and pulled from an unvalidated staging table. The agent didn't fail because of the model, or because it couldn't translate a user question into a query. It failed because it didn't understand your business . The real kicker is that understanding usually already exists in the form of a semantic model in a Looker, dbt, Snowflake, Databricks, or SAP system. But because each definition stays locked inside its own tool, every agent guesses at it… and often gets it wrong. This is where Knowledge Catalog comes in. It brings the semantic models from all of those tools into one context graph, so every agent works from the same trusted definitions. And when two tools define the same metric differently, both definitions appear with their provenance, so data stewards can reconcile the conflict before it reaches end users. Today, we're announcing the general availability of expanded semantic model support. Knowledge Catalog now natively ingests semantic models and metric definitions from Looker LookML, BigQuery Graph (including BigQuery measures), dbt MetricFlow, Snowflake Semantic Views, Databricks Metric Views, and SAP Core Schema Notation (CSN), and connects them with schema, lineage, data profiles, business glossary and other key metadata in a single context graph, without moving data or rewriting business logic in a new language. By grounding your AI agents in those models, they get the same business definitions your analysts rely on, so their answers line up with the numbers your business trusts. In fact, based on internal benchmarks, grounding agents in Knowledge Catalog makes them nearly 4X more accurate, with up to 33% lower latency, and using up to 75% fewer tokens. The unified context graph enables you to: Reuse the semantic models you already trust: Knowledge Catalog grounds Gemini agent, BigQuery Conversational Analytics, and your custom agents in the metrics, filters, and join paths your teams have already defined, wherever they live. Go beyond hand-curated definitions with self-learned context: Knowledge Catalog pairs the well-defined metrics and KPI definitions in your semantic models with relevant context it extracts from unstructured knowledge sources, such as operational playbooks, meeting notes, chat threads, code, and more. Powered by Gemini, self-learning enrichment continuously finds missing or outdated context and turns it into governed, reusable context sets, ensuring your agents' context stays current as definitions change, without relying only on manual curation. Pair business logic with enterprise trust: Even the right formula produces the wrong answer when it runs on stale or uncertified data. That's why Knowledge Catalog can connect semantic definition to data quality scores, freshness signals, and lineage, so an agent knows what it can trust before it writes a line of SQL. Side-by-side comparison of the same question in Gemini without Knowledge Catalog (left) and grounded in Knowledge Catalog (right). Highlights the grounded agent (right) giving an accurate response with less token and lower latency, compared to the agent without Knowledge Catalog (left) hallucinating and using more tokens with higher latency. One context graph across your data estate The context graph that Knowledge Catalog creates is a connected map of your data and semantic estate: tables, semantic models, glossary terms, and data products are nodes; lineage, associations, schema keys, joins mined from real query history, and the join paths declared in your semantic models are the edges. Ingested semantics land in that same graph, next to pre-existing governance and usage signals, so an agent moves from business concept to trusted formula and verified join paths in one traversal. Each source adds its own perspective on your business: Looker LookML (GA): Indexes models, explores, views, and dashboards using Live sync from Looker Core, capturing compiled metric SQL, fan-out-safe join conditions, mandatory filters, and lineage from source tables to executive dashboards. BigQuery Graph (GA): Indexes native property-graph definitions, node and edge tables, graph measures, and business synonyms, so agents reason over connected entities with Graph Query Language (GQL) traversals instead of brittle multi-table self-joins. dbt MetricFlow (GA): Links source objects to dbt models and MetricFlow metrics, alongside dbt data quality test results, filters, saved queries, freshness SLAs, and downstream exposures. Snowflake Semantic Views via Horizon Catalog (GA): Pairs federated BigQuery or Google Cloud Lakehouse tables with Snowflake Horizon metadata, bringing in Semantic View dimensions, facts, metric formulas, relationships, and synonyms, plus Data Metric Function quality scorecards and PII masking tags. Databricks Metric Views via Unity Catalog (GA): Ingests metric view definitions, measure formulas, scoping filters, and join cardinalities from Unity Catalog, alongside table certification badges and Lakehouse Monitoring profiling results. SAP Core Schema Notation (CSN) via SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) (GA): Captures business labels, dimension and cube modeling patterns, default aggregations, currency and unit bindings, key and composite join associations, and data sensitivity flags when SAP BDC Data Products are federated through Google Cloud Lakehouse. Because every source lands as a node or an edge in the same graph, a LookML join, a dbt exposure, a Snowflake relationship, or an SAP association are traversable side by side, with links tying each one back to the physical tables it depends on. And nothing is silently overwritten: overlapping definitions stay side by side, each labeled with its source, giving data stewards the full picture they need to settle on a single version. Navigating semantic models, join paths, and lineage on the context graph in Knowledge Studio. You can explore and govern all of this in Knowledge Studio (preview), your command center to explore and manage your context. Explore your context graph, including your semantic definitions, using natural language prompts and traverse connection paths using the context graph canvas. Then, once you've validated the right assets and definitions, you can package them into reusable context sets that map to specific use cases and domains in your organization, which Gemini and custom agents can consume in production. Get started Let’s get back to that net revenue question. With Knowledge Catalog, the VP of Sales’ agent issues a single context query to discover the trusted asset, applying the exact metric formula and filters that your domain experts defined, all while respecting join keys across systems, and confirming that the underlying data passed its quality checks. Better yet, the numbers in the report are correct! To get started, explore your context graph in Knowledge Studio and visit the Knowledge Catalog documentation to connect to more sources.
summary: Picture the scene: Before an executive business review, your VP of Sales asks an AI assistant, "What was net revenue for our top enterprise accounts last quarter?" In seconds, the agent returns a polished chart! Unfortunately, the numbers don't match the finance report. Why? Because the agent counted cancelled orders as revenue and pulled from an unvalidated staging table.

title: Introducing the AlloyDB Omni web UI for easier cluster observability
raw_text: Managing PostgreSQL databases across on-premises, edge, and multi-cloud environments often forces administrators to rely on command-line tools, making it hard to see cluster health and quickly diagnose issues. To solve this, we are announcing the General Availability (GA) of the AlloyDB Omni Web UI for Red Hat and containers . This production-ready, read-only console gives you direct visibility into hardware telemetry, query performance, and configuration flags for AlloyDB Omni so you can troubleshoot workloads quickly and safely without leaving your local or enterprise environment. What is AlloyDB Omni? AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, self-managed edition of AlloyDB that brings enterprise capabilities and full PostgreSQL compatibility to your own infrastructure. Built to run anywhere — across on-premises data centers, edge environments, and multi-cloud deployments — it includes built-in columnar acceleration and integrated AI tooling. With AlloyDB Omni, you can modernize demanding transactional and analytical workloads while retaining complete control over your operating environment. Key Web UI capabilities at a glance Cluster overview and profiles: Switch between target connection profiles quickly without using the command line. System monitoring: View real-time performance telemetry for CPU, memory, and disk I/O to plan capacity and triage infrastructure issues. Query performance: Identify resource-heavy SQL statements through a visual breakdown of database load, latency bottlenecks, and slow queries. Columnar Engine diagnostics: Track the in-memory columnar store, caching, and coverage to verify analytical query acceleration. Parameter and flag auditing: Inspect runtime database parameters centrally to identify configuration drift against your organizational baselines. AlloyDB AI and ecosystem shortcuts: Inspect vector search and AI workflows, and access quick launchpad shortcuts for ecosystem tools like pgBackRest. Production-safe diagnostics and profile management When you triage complex database workloads across bare-metal VMs, containers, or Kubernetes, you need a clear, isolated view of instance health. The Web UI provides a dedicated visual environment for this. Profile management: Store and toggle between saved connection profiles for local development, staging, or production environments. Read-only operations: The interface operates strictly in read-only mode, ensuring that diagnostic sessions cannot execute write commands or modify your underlying database configurations. Dual-layer observability: System and query monitoring To isolate production performance spikes, you need immediate visibility into both hardware health and SQL statement execution. System monitoring: The Web UI integrates with standard Prometheus telemetry to show you real-time CPU use, memory allocation, storage I/O, and active connection trends. Query monitoring: The dashboard automatically ranks execution-heavy SQL statements by total latency and call frequency. You can instantly isolate unindexed or resource-intensive queries to resolve issues faster. System Insights and Query Insights in AlloyDB Omni Web UI Real-time Columnar Engine diagnostics AlloyDB Omni includes an advanced Columnar Engine that organizes frequently accessed data in memory, accelerating analytical queries significantly compared to standard PostgreSQL. The Web UI helps you monitor this feature directly: Memory footprint tracking: Check real-time columnar memory consumption against your hardware limits. Columnarization and cache coverage: See exactly which tables and columns are actively cached in memory to confirm your workloads are running as fast as possible. AlloyDB AI and Columnar Engine Insights in AlloyDB Omni Web UI Database flag and parameter auditing Keeping database parameters uniform across distributed environments keeps your operations stable. The Web UI gives you a central catalog to inspect active database flags and runtime settings. You can verify node settings against your organizational policies without connecting to servers via SSH or parsing configuration files manually. If configuration drift is detected, changes should be applied via the authoritative provisioning workflow (e.g., updating Kubernetes CRDs/GitOps manifests, running Ansible playbooks, or using alloydbctl). Database flags in AlloyDB Omni Web UI Built-in AlloyDB AI and tooling hub As you build generative AI applications on top of PostgreSQL, the Web UI gives you direct visibility into vector search workflows and AI model integrations. You can also quickly navigate to documentation and external ecosystem resources, including backup tools like pgBackRest, directly from the console's tooling hub. Operational scope and prerequisites We designed the AlloyDB Omni Web UI with clear operational boundaries so you can deploy it easily within enterprise security boundaries and air-gapped environments. Non-Intrusive Monitoring: The interface operates with minimal permissions out of the box, preserving your existing command-line tools and CI/CD pipelines as the authoritative controls for cluster provisioning and administrative workflows. Standard monitoring prerequisites: To see complete system hardware metrics, you need standard Prometheus monitoring configured within your host environment. Get started Ready to modernize your PostgreSQL workloads and get dedicated observability for your AlloyDB Omni cluster ? Sign up for enterprise access: To request access to RPM-based enterprise distributions, advanced tooling, and the Web UI, complete the sign-up form for RPM based deployment of AlloyDB Omni. To request access to container-based enterprise distributions, advanced tooling, and the Web UI, complete the sign-up form for container-based deployment . Install the Web UI: Follow the step-by-step installation instructions in the AlloyDB Omni documentation to deploy the AlloyDB Omni Web UI For deployment using Red Hat RPM: Deploy via native RPM Package For deployment using Docker or Podman: Deploy via container image

title: Behind the scenes, two months later: How we ship Google Agent Skills like products
raw_text:
In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills , covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates that every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons that we learned along the way. You can adopt similar gates and review rules in your own skill repository. Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000. It now hosts over 170 skills from teams across Google, and we distribute them across multiple AI platforms. Building agent skills for a single developer or a small project is straightforward. You write a SKILL.md file, define a few instructions, test it manually, and it works. At our scale, manual workflows stop being effective. Unvetted edits can introduce subtle bugs, and it becomes difficult to catch issues before they reach users. The core philosophy: Ship skills like products One key lesson from my previous post: a skill is a living product, not a one-off document. In practice, that means we ship every skill update like a product release. It's tempting to treat a skill as documentation. But documentation explains concepts to a human reader, while a skill steers an AI agent's reasoning loop, tool selection, and execution path. A misplaced phrase in a skill can cause an agent to invoke invalid command flags, enter an infinite loop, or waste tokens. That makes every instruction edit a behavioral change. You wouldn't ship a product update without testing it, and the same goes for a skill. This principle drives three core requirements: Strict semantic versioning : Every behavioral change requires an explicit version bump. Deterministic automated validation : Linters and validators check every proposed change before a human or AI reviewer sees it. Mandatory evaluation evidence : Every change includes an evaluation report. It compares the skill against its previous version, or—if the skill is new—against an agent without the skill. Automated conformance gates: The pull request pipeline In my previous post, I briefly listed the checks that every skill passes on check-in: linters, link checkers, and AI-assisted checklists. Here's what's inside them, plus two gates that I haven't covered before: semantic versioning and evaluation suite validation. When an author submits a change to our internal skills repository, an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline triggers immediately. Before a skill is exported to GitHub, it must pass these six automated gates and receive human approval: Structural conformance : Directory layout, allowed files, and taxonomy. Skill linters : Frontmatter, folder naming, and Markdown rules. Semantic versioning : Version bump for every behavioral change. Evaluation suite : Valid eval suite and a fresh eval report. Link validation : Links are valid. AI review agent : Skill quality and design standards. Human approval : Final approval from a human reviewer (a subject matter expert) . Structural conformance and skill linters Our automated validation suite inspects every pull request for structural and syntactical correctness. Some of the rules include these requirements: Folder name and metadata name must match. SKILL.md and description length limits are enforced. All required fields in the frontmatter metadata are present. Only a curated list of files and directories is allowed within a skill directory. All Markdown files follow formatting rules. The main README.md file and the machine-readable index.json registry are up to date. Semantic versioning Every skill declares a semantic version in its SKILL.md frontmatter metadata: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '---
name: spanner-basics
metadata:
 version: "1.1.1"
 category: Databases
description: ...
---'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecd95cbd0>)])]> First, our automated checks verify that the version is a quoted string. YAML parses unquoted values like 2.0 as numbers, which causes unexpected parsing errors in tools that expect a string. Second, the validator checks the version transition itself. New skills must start at 1.0.0 , and any change to an existing skill's instructions, scripts, or references requires a version bump or the pull request is blocked. Standard reset rules apply: bumping MAJOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 2.0.0 ) resets MINOR and PATCH to 0 , and bumping MINOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 1.5.0 ) resets PATCH to 0 . Why enforce strict versioning if the agent only reads the Markdown instructions? The version number is for the developer and their package tooling, not for the model at runtime. Skills don't auto-update in the background, which means there's no network check or latency overhead each time an agent invokes a skill. Instead, explicit versions let developers compare their locally installed skills against the upstream catalog and decide when to pull changes—for example, by running the npx skills update command. This versioning also supports workflows where teams want to lock a critical skill to a known-good version to guarantee reproducible agent behavior across their projects. Evaluation suite validation Our continuous evaluations (evals) compare agent performance with and without each skill. Those results are only as reliable as the evaluation suites behind them. If a suite contains broken file references or compound expectations, test results become noisy and untrustworthy. Our validator parses each evaluation suite and the pull request description. Then it checks several strict invariants: Resolution of file-based prompts : When a test prompt references a file (such as @file:test_prompt.txt ), the validator confirms that the target file exists and that it isn't empty. Atomic expectations : Each expectation must check exactly one criterion. The validator blocks compound expectations until authors split them. Lesson 2 later in this post shows why. Duplicate detection : The validator flags duplicate test prompts and conflicting expectations within the same evaluation suite. Mandatory evaluation report : Every pull request that modifies a skill must link to an evaluation report in its description. Eval staleness check : Authors usually iterate on a pull request as reviewers leave feedback. The validator confirms that the linked report ran against the latest commit. Link validation Over 170 skills link to documentation for fast-evolving Google products, and those pages can move long after a skill passes review. Rather than waiting for users to report broken links, we validate links at two stages. Before merge, pull request checks verify all relative links, such as files in references/ . Then, every Monday, a GitHub Actions workflow runs lychee across all external links in the public repository and it reports any broken links to skill owners for remediation. AI review agent Linters and schema validators catch syntactic errors, but they can't evaluate overall quality. They can't tell you if an instruction is confusing, if a reference guide is too verbose, or if a task should have been a bash script instead of a large language model (LLM) instruction. To solve this, we integrated an AI review agent into our review pipeline. When a change affects a skill, the AI reviewer inspects it using a dedicated review skill. Yes, we use a skill to review skills. Here are the core rules the AI reviewer evaluates. You can adopt these rules in your own skill development workflows. 1. Skill suitability and the deterministic trap The first question our AI reviewer asks is simple: Does this task belong in an instruction? We often see authors fall into the deterministic trap . They write rigid, numbered sequences of command-line interface (CLI) commands directly into Markdown text. LLMs are probabilistic engines. If an operation requires a strict sequence of commands where a variation can cause an error, embedding those commands in the instruction text invites hallucinations. Our AI reviewer enforces a clear boundary between deterministic and probabilistic logic. Rigid CLI sequences, JSON parsers, and deployment steps must live in executable scripts under scripts/ . Markdown instructions are reserved for tasks that require judgment, such as choosing an architecture, diagnosing error logs, or synthesizing code. This rule complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) guidance that I shared last time: prefer remote MCP tools whenever possible. When you must fall back to CLI or API calls, wrap them in a script instead of spelling them out in the instructions. 2. The L1/L2/L3 modular architecture Context windows are valuable. Loading a 2,000-line skill into an agent consumes context and degrades reasoning. Our AI reviewer enforces a three-tier information hierarchy that follows the progressive disclosure model of Agent Skills: Level 1 (Metadata) : The YAML frontmatter ( name , description ). The agent uses this concise summary for discovery and routing. Level 2 (Core instructions) : The main SKILL.md file. The body must stay compact (under 500 lines). It provides workflow overviews, decision trees, and guardrails. Level 3 (Reference docs) : Detailed API references, schemas, and other reference tables live in a references/ directory. Our AI reviewer enforces two distinct rules for Level 3: flat directory structure and single-hop indirection . Keeping references/ flat (no subdirectories) is a repository convention that discourages sprawling documentation trees and makes file discovery simpler. More importantly for runtime performance, the reviewer blocks chained references , where SKILL.md links to a reference file that links to yet another file. Each hop requires an extra tool call, adding latency and cost, and our evaluations showed that agents frequently stop before following a second level of chained references. 3. Non-interactive script design When skills bundle helper scripts in scripts/ , we expect agents to execute them directly in terminal sandboxes. Our AI reviewer flags any script that blocks on interactive prompts. Every script must accept inputs through command-line flags or environment variables, provide --help documentation, and include a --dry-run or confirmation flag for destructive operations. Scripts also need to separate output cleanly, writing structured data (usually JSON) to standard output and writing actionable error messages to standard error. Example AI review checklist snippet The review skill also checks frontmatter for spec compliance and discovery, and it turns the L1/L2/L3 architecture into concrete structure rules. Here's an excerpt from those criteria: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '### Front Matter & Discovery

- **Spec Compliance**: YAML front matter MUST strictly follow the Agent Skills
 Reference Specification (https://agentskills.io/specification). Use `>-`
 (folded strip-chomping) format for multi-line descriptions.
- **Description Quality**: The `description` field must follow the
 [Description Guide](references/description_guide.md).

### Content Structure & Authoring Quality

- **L1/L2/L3 Architecture**: Enforce modular structure. The main `SKILL.md`
 body must stay under 500 lines. Move deep domain reference material to
 `references/` (see [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
- **Flat References Directory**: `references/` must be a flat directory (one
 level deep, no nested subdirectories). References > 100 lines must include a
 Table of Contents with line hints (see
 [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
- **Avoid Deeply-Nested References**: Avoid deeply-nested references (e.g.,
 `SKILL.md` -> `references/guides.md` -> `assets/output.tmpl`). Keep
 reference structures shallow (one level of indirection from `SKILL.md`)
 because agents might not load such link targets fully.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecdabcc10>)])]> Human approval After it passes all automated checks, every pull request must receive approval from a human reviewer. The reviewer is typically the skill's subject matter expert and, for new skills, a member of the Central Skills team. Lessons learned from repository history Six months of commit history and pull request discussions reveal several practical takeaways. 1. Scope CI checks carefully Early in the project, we configured automated pull request checks with broad directory patterns. One check required an approved bug tracking ticket on every change. Because the pattern matched too broadly, engineers making a one-line typo fix were blocked for missing a tracking ticket. Meanwhile, newly added skills in deeper subdirectories went uninspected. Takeaway : Match automated check rules to specific file operations, such as added versus modified files, and verify exact path depths. Treat minor edits to existing skills differently from new skills. 2. Atomic expectations When we started writing evaluation suites, we saw authors write compound expectations like this: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Bad: Compound expectation
- "The agent must create a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1, enable
 uniform bucket-level access, and apply lifecycle rules."'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecdabd390>)])]> If the agent configured the region and lifecycle rules but missed the uniform access flag, the LLM-as-a-judge scorer returned inconsistent ratings. Migrating to atomic expectations resolved the inconsistent ratings: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Good: Atomic expectations
- "The agent specifies us-central1 for the bucket location."
- "The agent enables uniform bucket-level access on the created bucket."
- "The agent defines a lifecycle configuration rule deleting objects
 older than 30 days."'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbecdabd210>)])]> Takeaway : Check exactly one criterion per expectation. Atomic expectations make evaluation results clear, reliable, and debuggable. 3. Documentation drift happens fast In a multi-contributor repository, documentation tables drift within days if maintained manually. Takeaway : If you publish an index or catalog, never rely on contributors to update it manually. Instead, write a generator script and enforce it with a CI unit test. That's the origin of the README.md and index.json checks in our linters. Our index.json even opens with a warning: "This file is generated. Do not edit it by hand." 4. Gate expensive LLM checks behind fast deterministic ones Running full evaluation suites and an AI review agent on every change can get expensive fast, both in token usage and CI runtime—especially when authors push frequent small commits during review. In our pipeline, fast deterministic checks run first. Structural conformance, skill linters, and semantic versioning act as blocking gates: if any of them fail, the pipeline stops immediately and it won't trigger the AI reviewer or evaluation checks until those issues are fixed. Takeaway : Stage your pipeline so cheap, deterministic checks block broken changes before LLM-powered gates run. When you build a similar system, consider adding further cost guardrails, such as manual triggers for heavy checks (for example, a /run-evals pull request comment) or only triggering automatic re-runs when the diff exceeds a specific threshold. Conclusion Building a scalable Agent Skills repository requires more than good prompt engineering. It requires solid developer infrastructure: Ship skills like products: version, validate, and evaluate every change. Enforce semantic versioning and atomic expectations with automated CI gates. Use an AI reviewer to catch design anti-patterns, such as the deterministic trap. Check links before merge and on a schedule. Links and further reading To get started with Google Agent Skills, check out these resources: Google Agent Skills repo : github.com/google/skills Previous post : Behind the scenes: How we build, test, and scale Google Agent Skills Launch announcement : Level Up Your Agents: Announcing Google's Official Skills Repository Skills tutorial : Introduction: What Are Google Cloud Agent Skills? What's next? If you found this post helpful, share it with your friends on social media and connect with me on LinkedIn , X , or Bluesky . Thanks for reading!

title: How to troubleshoot GKE workloads faster with VPC Flow Logs
raw_text: Having visibility into your network traffic is essential to operating Kubernetes environments effectively. When a service slows down or loses connectivity, knowing who is talking to whom lets you narrow the problem down quickly. In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols. In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary. Their IP addresses change constantly as pods scale, crash, or move between nodes, so a raw log entry showing 10.4.2.18 talking to 10.4.8.44 tells you little about which workload (and pod) owned that address, what namespace it was in, or what application it was trying to reach. By the time you search your cluster, the pod may already be gone! In a Google Cloud environment, VPC Flow Logs closes this gap at the network layer. Google Cloud's virtual network already sees every connection a pod makes, so each sampled flow is recorded with the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) metadata behind the IP address: pod, workload, namespace, and service. You get workload-level attribution for L3/L4 traffic without deploying extra agents or sidecars, and it complements in-cluster Container Network Interface (CNI) and dataplane observability tools you may already run when you need deeper detail. Let’s take a deeper look at how VPC Flow Logs and GKE work together, and how to get started with it. How GKE metadata enriches VPC Flow Logs VPC Flow Logs samples traffic directly inside Google Cloud's virtual network. When flow logs are enabled for a subnet that hosts a GKE cluster, every record of pod traffic that passes through the VPC network is annotated with the Kubernetes context that owned the IP address at the time of sampling. This helps ensure the context is preserved even after the pod is gone: Cluster: The cluster name and location. Workload: The pod name and namespace, along with the controller that owns the pod, such as a deployment, StatefulSet, or DaemonSet. Service name: The Kubernetes service that received the traffic. Node and zone: The standard VPC fields, including the node VM and its zone on both ends of the flow. If you register your GKE workloads in App Hub , each record also carries application-level labels ( apphubSource and apphubDestination ) that identify the business application, environment, and criticality of each endpoint. This is especially useful when GKE microservices talk to App Hub-registered resources outside the cluster, such as Cloud Run services. Before you start Upgrade your log bucket to Observability Analytics (formerly Log Analytics): Flow Analyzer reads only from an upgraded bucket, typically _Default . Note: This upgrade is permanent. gcloud logging buckets update _Default \ --location=global \ --enable-analytics Enable VPC Flow Logs organization-wide: One organization-level configuration covers every subnet in every VPC network, including future clusters (requires Network Management Admin role). Keep include-all-metadata on so every record carries namespace and pod details. To balance visibility against cost, you can add a secondary sampling rate ( --flow-sampling ), an aggregation interval ( --aggregation-interval ), or a filter expression ( --filter-expr ) to view only the traffic of interest. gcloud network-management vpc-flow-logs-configs create CONFIG_NAME \ --location=global \ --organization=ORGANIZATION_ID \ --metadata=include-all-metadata Turn on intranode visibility : Autopilot clusters already have it, but you need to enable it on Standard clusters. Note: Enabling it restarts control plane and node components and adds some per-node overhead, so test it on a non-production cluster first. gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER_NAME \ --location=LOCATION \ --enable-intra-node-visibility Now you’re ready to get started. Analyze traffic visually in Flow Analyzer VPC Flow Logs write every record to Cloud Logging, you can search and query it in Logs Explorer or Log Analytics. For day-to-day work, Flow Analyzer , part of Network Intelligence Center, turns the same records into an interactive chart and table, so you can group and filter traffic by cluster, namespace, workload, pod, or service in a few clicks. The walkthroughs below use Online Boutique , an open-source microservices demo, on a GKE Autopilot cluster in us-central1. A loadgenerator deployment sends synthetic shopper traffic to the frontend , which calls productcatalogservice , cartservice , currencyservice , recommendationservice , shippingservice , adservice , and checkoutservice . Case 1: Turn IP addresses into workload names Whether you’re investigating an incident or assessing an architecture change, the first question is always the same: Which endpoints are communicating, and at what volume? Rather than presenting ephemeral IP address pairs, GKE metadata allows Flow Analyzer to answer this question directly using Kubernetes workload names. Steps in Flow Analyzer: Open Network Intelligence Center > Flow Analyzer and set the time range to last 1 hour . Under Source and Destination , set Organize flows by to GKE workload. In the filter bar, add the GKE workload is known filter so only pod-to-pod traffic is shown. Click Run new query . Grouping traffic by Source GKE workload and Destination GKE workload in Flow Analyzer to map microservice dependencies without raw IP lookups. Key insights: Sorted by volume, the table is a ready-made application dependency map: frontend handles incoming requests from loadgenerator (representing user traffic), while productcatalogservice answers calls from both recommendationservice and frontend . Because each row shows workload names instead of raw IP addresses, any unauthorized or unexpected workload-to-workload communication immediately becomes apparent. Case 2: Drill into a single service When a service is slow or about to change, you need to know who depends on it and how heavily. Steps in Flow Analyzer: Change Traffic aggregation to Client ↔ server (bidirectional) , so requests and responses between a pair are counted together. Under Server , add the filter GKE workload = productcatalogservice . Click Run new query , then click Details on the top row. Filtering on Server GKE workload (productcatalogservice) with Client ↔ server (bidirectional) aggregation to view caller share and the Details timeline. Key insights: You get every caller of the catalog service, each caller's share of its traffic, and a timeline for every pair, so if one caller's line climbs while the others stay flat, you know where to look first. When the question is latency rather than volume, switch the display mode to latency to rank the same callers by round-trip time. Case 3: Find the pods that talk across zones In a regional GKE cluster, chatty services that land in different zones send every request across a zone boundary, adding inter-zone data transfer charges. Because VPC Flow Logs record the zone at both ends of every flow, the pod pairs driving that traffic are easy to spot. Steps in Flow Analyzer: Switch from Basic filters to SQL filters , which let you compare two fields of the same flow. In the WHERE box, enter src_gcp_zone <> dest_gcp_zone . Set Organize flows by to Source GCP zone, Source GKE pod, Destination GCP zone , and Destination GKE pod . Click Run new query . Using SQL filters with src_gcp_zone <> dest_gcp_zone and multi-attribute grouping to identify pod pairs driving cross-zone network traffic. Key insights: The table displays cross-zone traffic ranked by volume, identifying the exact pods and zones on each end. In our cluster, the top flows occur between a frontend pod in us-central1-b and a currencyservice pod in us-central1-c, followed by checkoutservice , shippingservice , and productcatalogservice pairs. To investigate further, click Explore in Log Analytics to open the underlying SQL query for additional customization, such as adding joins or time buckets. GKE has a built-in answer: set trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone ( PreferClose on older versions) on the Service to prefer healthy endpoints in the caller's zone, and make sure each zone has enough replicas to serve its own traffic. What to keep in mind Pod-to-internet traffic: VPC Flow Logs carry no pod annotations, because the masquerade agent replaces the pod IP with the node IP before the flow is sampled. Keeping internal destinations in the non-masquerade list preserves pod names for those flows, and if you run ip-masq-agent with intranode visibility, that list must also include the cluster's node and pod IP ranges to avoid connectivity problems. Blocked traffic: Traffic blocked by a network policy never reaches the VPC network, so use NetworkPolicy logging to investigate it. Sampling: Flow logs are sampled, which makes byte and packet counts well suited for ranking and trending rather than per-connection accounting. Next steps If your clusters already have VPC Flow Logs turned on, upgrading the _Default bucket and opening Flow Analyzer is all it takes to reproduce the three walkthroughs above. To learn more, see the documentation: Using VPC Flow Logs VPC Flow Logs record format for GKE Analyzing network traffic with Flow Analyzer Best practices for GKE network observability Troubleshooting GKE network observability
summary: Having visibility into your network traffic is essential to operating Kubernetes environments effectively. When a service slows down or loses connectivity, knowing who is talking to whom lets you narrow the problem down quickly. In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols. In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary.

title: How GKE networking scales to support high densities of concurrent AI agents
raw_text: What do you need to orchestrate high-density concurrent AI agents? As we transition from static requests toward autonomous agentic workflows, the need for secure, high-density sandboxes is pushing conventional infrastructure far beyond its architectural breaking point. This transition is driving top-tier research labs to demand infrastructure at unprecedented scale — often up to one million concurrent code-execution sandboxes! At this scale, the efficiency of your Kubernetes networking infrastructure directly impacts the economic viability of an agentic initiative. In advanced workflows like reinforcement learning (RL), extreme pod churn can mean thousands of isolated sandboxes spinning up and down every minute. To make sure that valuable GPUs and TPUs are spending their time executing models rather than waiting on sandboxes to initialize, you need sub-second provisioning and extreme compute density. By providing secure, lightweight isolation, Agent Sandbox on GKE is uniquely positioned to power these highly dynamic execution environments. Furthermore, for next-generation workloads with millions of concurrent idle sessions, Agent Substrate on GKE builds on these primitives to deliver even greater density and sub-second state rehydration. In this post, you will learn how GKE Dataplane V2 optimizes network identity management, solves identity scaling limits, and enables sub-second provisioning to power high-density, large-scale AI agent workloads. A common scale challenge: network identity management Operating with massive concurrency introduces fascinating new engineering challenges, particularly in how you manage network identities. Traditionally, custom controllers and workload orchestrators often assign unique, dynamic labels to each pod (such as agent-id, timestamps, or claim-uid). GKE Dataplane V2 , powered by eBPF technology, helps enforce robust network security policies by mapping pod labels to a numeric identity. Because agentic workflows generate highly unique labels for every pod, the system proactively provisions a distinct identity for each sandbox. In a rapidly changing environment, this serial allocation process can briefly pause pod creation as the system securely updates eBPF maps, occasionally leading to slower-than-desired initialization. Additionally, sophisticated workloads can approach the cluster-wide limit of 65,536 network identities, either through this rapid generation or overall scale of the workload itself. GKE network dataplane innovations for an agentic world Providing a reliable and highly secure platform is fundamental to everything we do. As such, we needed to find a way to provide the same underlying identity and security controls while providing higher scalability and performance. That's where the architectural innovations in GKE Dataplane V2 come in. A customer has testified to the success of Agent Substrate on GKE to orchestrate hundreds of thousands of secure environments across clusters and handle spikes of over 30,000 sandboxes on a single cluster. To achieve this, GKE relies on a two-pronged networking approach: Migrating high-cardinality data Google's GKE Dataplane V2 separates "identifying" data from "functional" metadata. Ensure your fields that do not actively participate in service selector matching or core resource grouping are migrated from the Pod's Labels set to the Annotations set. GKE Dataplane V2 intelligently calculates network identities based on labels rather than annotations, moving this high-cardinality metadata out of the labels completely bypasses the need for per-Pod identity generation. This elegant shift natively resolves identity scaling limits without sacrificing visibility. Advanced Cilium label filtering In addition, applying precise label exclusion filters (e.g., using the cilium-config-emergency-override ConfigMap in kube-system ) by configuring rules like !agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash or !timestamp , these explicitly instruct GKE Dataplane V2 to gracefully ignore these dynamic labels during security identity calculation. This means that even if a developer framework inadvertently introduces high-cardinality labels, configuring appropriate exclusion filters allows Google’s network dataplane to drop them automatically. As a result, identical agent types continue sharing a single Cilium pod identity, maintaining the ultra-low-latency startup times critical for dynamic AI workloads. By preventing linear identity growth and avoiding Cilium’s 65,536 identity limit, GKE provides leading speed and efficiency for fully isolated agents with 300 sandboxes per second at sub-second latency. Looking ahead For workloads that require extreme performance, scale, and density, Agent Substrate natively integrates these GKE Dataplane V2 recommendations while bypassing Kubernetes scheduling limits, pushing GKE’s performance and scale even further. In benchmark validation running 200,000 agents, Agent Substrate sustained 500 activations per second at less than 500 ms suspend and resume latency. You can deploy it on your existing GKE clusters today to minimize idle compute costs for your most demanding AI workflows. By optimizing network identity calculation and filtering high-cardinality metadata, GKE Dataplane V2 addresses critical infrastructure bottlenecks in large-scale AI workloads. These architectural improvements reduce sandbox provisioning latency to sub-second levels, minimize expensive GPU idle times, and help maintain high compute density. Ultimately, these efficiencies let you scale your agentic AI operations reliably while controlling operational costs. To learn more, explore Agent Sandbox and Agent Substrate on GKE.
