title: Fake Anthropic AI previews lure in overeager employees
raw_text: Everyone wants to know what Anthropic is up to, and hackers are gleefully exploiting the fact. New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterprise users by making them think they are getting an invite to a private invite-only Anthropic preview. In reality, adversarial actors are trying to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials, exploiting video teleconferencing software GoTo Webinar branding to do so. “It sells exclusivity,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Fear of missing out is the oldest lure in the book.” Every organization is trying to figure out where AI fits, he noted, and a private preview of Anthropic’s newest technology is exactly the invitation an ambitious employee would want to accept. “The attackers did not pick Anthropic at random,” he said. “They picked whatever is hottest in the news cycle. Next month, it may be another name.” How attackers lure users with spoofed Anthropic invites GoTo Webinar is a widely used platform, and its meeting invitation emails are typically not blocked by security tools . The Cofense researchers found that attackers are exploiting this fact by sending what seems to be an invitation email from a legitimate sender; when users click on the link to register for the fake webinar, they are instead sent to a compromised URL. The email offers what the researchers call a “tantalizing” offer: “This private, invitation-only virtual session brings together a select group of participants to a focused conversation on AI systems, research, and the future of frontier models,” it reads. A URL shortener circumvents email security tools, and the attackers use subdomains and dashes (-) to hide the malicious URL. The link itself appears to have been generated by Zapier, a legitimate company whose tools are designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI compatible with Model Context Protocol (MCP). The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com (GoTo Webinar’s website is actually www.goto.com ). The text contains no obvious spelling errors, and the email contains GoTo Webinar branding. However, the researchers noted, the email sender’s name is “Austin from nthropic,” with the “A” missing. “Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign,” they pointed out. If the phishing link is clicked, a Cloudflare CAPTCHA page appears, and must be completed before the login prompt is presented. This serves as the first of two checkpoints to prevent security tools from scanning attackers’ websites. “Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure,” the researchers explained. Once the CAPTCHA is completed, victims are led to a Zoom-spoofing invitation page. If they want to “attend” the fake event, they must register, and they are prompted to enter their work email address. When they click “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft,” yet another CAPTCHA page appears. Both CAPTCHA pages seem to be good at detecting and blocking analysis by VPN services, scanners, Tor browsers, and other security tools, the researchers noted. Also, because there are two distinct CAPTCHA pages, such tools may not be able to follow every step in the attack. “A CAPTCHA was built to keep bots out,” Dickson pointed out. “Here, it keeps the security scanners out and lets the victims in.” The fake Google and Microsoft login pages differ a bit, however. The spoofed Google page does not capture passwords, only usernames, which the researchers surmise is due to a misconfiguration; the spoofed Microsoft page does collect both usernames and passwords. But both are “remarkably similar” to their respective legitimate pages, and their subdomains are “tricky.” The fake Google URL is goo[.]gle-access-eventregister[.]icu, while the Microsoft URL closely mimics real Office and Sharepoint domains, using office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com. Once credentials are submitted, neither login offers a confirmation message, nor does it redirect to legitimate vendor pages. But by that point, attackers have already succeeded at exfiltrating credentials. That means they could compromise an account, access the sensitive documents in that account, or use it as an initial attack vector to further infiltrate the enterprise, the researchers explained. They advised checking if the branding of a message remains consistent from the email to a login page, searching for small inconsistencies such as minor misspellings, and reminding employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate. “Although the logos and design of the page may look correct, threat actors are skilled at mimicry, especially now with the use of AI,” the researchers noted. It’s not the employees’ fault The AI industry’s habit of gated previews and waitlists does not help in these situations, Dickson noted; it trains people to expect exactly this kind of invitation. “Start with the cracks the attackers left showing,” he advised: The sender supposedly came from “nthropic,” the email carried GoTo Webinar branding, the registration spoofed a Zoom meeting page, and the login pages were from Google or Microsoft. That’s three brands in three clicks, he noted. The fake login domains, like office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com, are built to be skimmed, not read, he pointed out. And, while the Google page collected only usernames, which may be a configuration error, the threat actors behind this campaign will likely fix that. “Training helps, but I would not hang the defense on an employee squinting at a URL at 4:45 on a Friday,” Dickson said; how much a stolen password is worth is a leadership decision, not a test the employee fails. Phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) such as passkeys makes a stolen password far less valuable, he noted. But enterprises ultimately have a short to-do list to allow them to defend themselves from this sort of scam, Dickson said: Verify any AI preview invitation through an account team or a known contact. Treat branding that changes from email to meeting page to login page as a red flag. Roll out phishing-resistant MFA. If someone entered credentials on one of these phishing login pages, reset them and review that account’s activity. “Bottom line: This campaign uses trusted tools to defeat defenses built on trust,” Dickson said. “The employee should not be the last line of defense.”
summary: Everyone wants to know what Anthropic is up to, and hackers are gleefully exploiting the fact. New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterprise users by making them think they are getting an invite to a private invite-only Anthropic preview. In reality, adversarial actors are trying to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials, exploiting video teleconferencing software GoTo Webinar branding to do so. “It sells exclusivity,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

title: Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
raw_text: OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls. The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions. “If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote in its October 15 submission. OpenAI, in its October 20 letter , called for an amendment to California’s Senate Bill 53 (SB 53). “We support amending SB 53 to require frontier developers to maintain effective shutdown controls and an enforceable duty to use them when unsafe conditions arise, and no lesser intervention would adequately address the risk,” OpenAI wrote. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the two approaches address complementary needs. “The operator must contain the unsafe activity promptly. Independent review must examine both intervention and inaction,” he said. Newsom’s executive order , N-9-26, directs California’s Government Operations Agency, in consultation with the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and national experts, to submit recommendations by November 16 on potential amendments to existing AI safety laws. The order asks officials to examine independent verification inside AI laboratories, independent checks of safety assessments, verified shutdown mechanisms, and expanded reporting of critical safety incidents. It does not itself impose these proposed requirements. Independent verification Anthropic wants evaluators to assess developers’ safety claims and publish their own findings. “We strongly support requiring independent verification of what frontier AI companies report about the risks of their models and whether those risks are sufficiently mitigated,” the company wrote. It proposed requiring developers to publish risk reports at least every six months, covering serious risks from their models, including internally used models substantially riskier than released systems. Evaluators should receive unredacted reports and access to developers’ most capable models and relevant internal information. Anthropic also proposed that developers pay into a state-administered pooled fund to finance evaluators, rather than pay them directly. It said a team from the independent evaluation organization METR had received employee-like access on a pilot basis, with further partnerships involving SecureBio and Accenture under development. OpenAI, in its letter, said it supports independent technical assessments but distinguishes them from compliance audits. Technical assessments would examine evidence behind developers’ safety claims and the effectiveness of safeguards; compliance audits would check whether companies follow their published safety frameworks and legal obligations, it added. OpenAI recommended annual independent compliance audits and focused technical assessments of serious risks arising during model training, evaluation and internal deployment. It also urged California to work with the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop common assessment standards. Gogia said oversight requires more than funding. “Credible assurance must survive an adverse finding,” he said. Beyond a single switch OpenAI argued that a single kill switch would not address the different ways AI systems operate and are deployed. “We recommend using the term ‘shutdown controls’ because it will require the development of multiple controls and coordinated action by different actors to stop AI operations when necessary, rather than a single switch,” the company wrote in the letter. Interventions could include stopping a training run, isolating an AI agent, revoking tool or network access, or suspending a service. OpenAI said responsibilities should extend to inference providers and downstream deployers according to the operations they control. It also noted that developers cannot reliably switch off independently operated copies of open-weight models running on external systems. Anthropic similarly argued for more targeted safeguards. “We think a more apt metaphor for what frontier AI companies need to build is a circuit breaker,” it wrote, advocating controls that can contain problems at the level of an agent, customer, deployment environment, or model. For enterprises, Gogia said, contractual shutdown responsibilities should match the controls each party actually possesses. Agreements should specify intervention authority, incident-reporting cooperation, and who can authorize a restart. “Every assigned duty needs an executable control,” he said, adding that CIOs should test recovery processes rather than assume switching to an alternative model will preserve safe operations. Both companies also called for broader reporting of incidents involving models that circumvent safeguards or take unauthorized actions. The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld .
summary: OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls. The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions. “If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote in its October 15 submission.

title: Imposter abused trust in OpenAI, Anthropic, and 30 others to hunt for secrets
raw_text: Attackers are impersonating AI agents from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in a bid to trick organizations into exposing sensitive credentials, according to researchers who observed a single threat actor cycling through dozens of fake bot identities while probing enterprise web servers for secrets. A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. A malicious scanner used by the attacker ran from an unnamed major cloud provider. “It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths,” Cequence’s director of threat research, Will Glazier, said in a blog post . Collin Hogue-Spears , senior director of solution management at Black Duck, who reviewed Cequence’s findings, points out that the scanner tested whether websites treated an AI bot’s self-declared name as proof of its identity. “The user-agent header is where a visitor names itself, and setting it costs nothing,” he said. Glazier said defending against such impersonation requires verifying every claimed identity before trusting it. While Cequence confirmed observing extensive scanning activity attributed to a single threat actor, it did not report a breach. “On one day in October, the actor reached 48% of the Cequence-protected organizations that saw any AI bot traffic,” the company said. A rotating cast of AI identities hunts for secrets According to Glazier, the scanner cycled through roughly 32 AI bot identities and targeted organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software. The activity was observed from at least late September through late October 2026. Instead of crawling publicly accessible pages, the scanner requested sensitive paths associated with configuration and credential files. Working through a list of approximately 90 file paths, it sent bursts of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds before moving on, Cequence said. The same bot machine was observed claiming to represent OpenAI , Anthropic, Meta, and Perplexity within seconds. It also used more than 300 cloud addresses in a single day, making static IP blocklists less effective as a standalone defense. “Fraud is now polymorphic: AI lets attackers vary their approach every time, so legacy, static fraud defenses decay faster than teams can update them,” warned Patrick Harr , chief executive officer at DataVisor. However, institutions that make real-time decisioning the foundation, with detection that adapts as quickly as the threats do, can use AI to defend as effectively as attackers do, he noted. Nearly all the scanner’s requests were blocked or failed, Cequence noted. Don’t trust the agent’s name, verify it Cequence recommends verifying AI crawlers through published address ranges, signed requests, or direct integrations rather than relying on self reported identities. Security teams should also flag bots that request credential files, keep secrets out of web-accessible directories, and assess automated traffic based on its behavior. Shane Barney , chief information security officer at Keeper Security, said organizations must extend zero-trust controls and least-privilege policies to AI agents, API keys, and service accounts. He also urged businesses to replace long-lived local credentials with centrally managed secrets. “When an identity starts looking for sensitive files it shouldn’t need, real-time threat detection must flag and terminate that machine session instantly,” Barney added.
summary: Attackers are impersonating AI agents from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in a bid to trick organizations into exposing sensitive credentials, according to researchers who observed a single threat actor cycling through dozens of fake bot identities while probing enterprise web servers for secrets. A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. A malicious scanner used by the attacker ran from an unnamed major cloud provider.

title: Vulnerability exploitation rising as the root cause of many breaches
raw_text: More evidence has emerged that attackers are turning to vulnerabilities rather than phishing as a means for breaking into corporate systems. Incident response firm LevelBlue’s Q3 findings show that vulnerability exploitation accounted for 14% of initial access cases, up from 4% in Q2. The finding represents more of a comeback than a fresh surge because in Q1 LevelBlue already recorded vulnerabilities as the root cause in 20% of the intrusions it investigated. In both Q1 and the latest figures known security vulnerabilities in edge devices made them the prime target for exploitation. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report — which is based on the combined evidence of multiple incident response vendors and law enforcement agencies — placed exploitation at the center of nearly a third (31%) of breaches, up from 20% the year before and ahead of credential abuse for the first time. Phishing/social engineering remain the top initial intrusion vector, accounting for 42% of breaches, down from 65% in Q2, according to LevelBlue’s Q3 report. Living on the edge Scott Doerr, experienced CISO turned founder of ForeGuard Advisory Group, said the biggest driver of the trend is exploitation of security flaws in internet-facing edge devices such as VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances. “LevelBlue’s most-exploited CVE lists this year are dominated by those appliances from SonicWall, Fortinet, Palo Alto, Ivanti, and BeyondTrust,” said Doerr. “They’re exposed by design, and a working exploit puts the attacker directly on the network with no user to fool and often no MFA prompt in the way.” Mitchell Spicer, co-founder and COO of Revelion AI, an autonomous AI penetration-testing platform, backed this assessment. “Phishing is still a major threat, but exploiting a vulnerability can give an attacker a direct route into a system without needing to persuade an employee to click a link,” said Spicer. “The opportunity is particularly attractive when organizations have internet-facing services that are unpatched, misconfigured, or forgotten.” AI offers a double-edged sword AI is adding another dimension to the cat and mouse game between attackers and enterprise security defenders. “It [AI] is making parts of reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery cheaper and more accessible, which can help defenders find weaknesses but can also help attackers identify potential targets,” Spicer said. “The longer those weaknesses remain exposed, the more opportunity attackers have to find and exploit them.”

The finding represents more of a comeback than a fresh surge because in Q1 LevelBlue already recorded vulnerabilities as the root cause in 20% of the intrusions it investigated. In both Q1 and the latest figures known security vulnerabilities in edge devices made them the prime target for exploitation.

title: Securing MCP servers before the AI rollout outpaces security
raw_text: Your company’s CTO has a plan to implement your company’s first LLM-based application. The board approved it, and now you’re finding out about it. It’s a typical story I hear all the time, and I’ve lived it myself. You’ve heard everything about models and LLMs, but now you see this new term all over the place: Model Context Protocol ( MCP ) servers —and the realization that you now need to make sure they are implemented securely. What is an MCP server? MCP servers are like the ODBC of the 1990s. Before ODBC , every application needed custom code to query databases. ODBC defined a single standard on how to talk to databases, and database vendors just developed a driver to talk to their solution. MCP servers work in the same way: the AI app just needs to use the standardized methods to communicate with the local MCP host, and each available tool (databases, file shares, CRMs) provides an MCP server that translates the MCP transmissions into the tool’s native format. So, you just need a driver on your MCP host to talk to any available endpoint. Fig.1 – MCP architecture. Greg Neville The MCP Hosts will be in your environment, and you can control the ingress and egress traffic allowed for each MCP Host. One MCP Host can also access more than one MCP Server, allowing greater scalability, but it also adds risk. Fig. 2 – Example marketing LLM application. Greg Neville Top priority MCP controls At this stage, define requirements before the MCP server implementation gets too far. Establish a list of requirements for the initial phase. Focus on the controls that deliver the most value and reduce the most risk. Input validation and sanitization Inputs from any indirect external sources outside your control are untrusted and should be treated as high-risk for abuse. Identifying and removing malicious input is vital for preventing misuse of an LLM application. Input validation and sanitization include strong authentication and authorization, detection of malicious code and jailbreak attempts, and filtering sensitive or regulated data. Output validation and sanitization These controls often involve enforcing a specific structure to facilitate validation, context-aware encoding and removal of unusual or unapproved data. Incorporate human oversight for higher-risk actions or other high-importance outputs, such as financial reporting. Network segmentation Segmenting MCP hosts can reduce the attack surface and limit potential abuse by restricting ingress and egress traffic to authorized systems and ports. Server hardening Servers should be configured following comprehensive guidelines such as the CIS Model . Hardening measures include disabling unnecessary or default accounts, closing unused ports and adjusting system settings to minimize vulnerabilities. Ideally, use infrastructure-as-code (IaaC) to make these servers ephemeral and further reduce the risk of a compromise spreading. Least access principle Permissions will be key in limiting the blast radius of what an attacker can do. Multiple MCP servers can be used to reduce over-permission by grouping tools that have similar access needs. Limit access to only the users, tenants and workloads that the server needs to provide the service. Also, limit token life to as short as possible in case any token is stolen. Encryption Encryption is hopefully a part of the server hardening process but needs to be called out on its own. Deploy encryption at rest and in transit end-to-end, with strong key management practices. Tool management Limiting the number of available tools on MCP hosts and restricting their capabilities to the minimum necessary can help reduce risks related to tool misuse and compromise. Third-party assessments and contracts Ensure third-party providers implement appropriate security controls, preferably verified by independent bodies such as SOC 2, HITRUST or ISO 27001/2 . Contracts should specify control requirements, and any identified high-risk gaps should be addressed through remediation agreements. A Business Associate Agreement ( BAA ) should be in place if protected health information (PHI) is involved. Audit and logging Maintaining detailed logs of AI actions and prompts is crucial for detecting issues like hacking attempts, AI misuse and prompt abuse. Human-in-the-loop Human-in-the-loop is critical for any high-risk action that an LLM application may try to take, or any highly critical data that is produced. Verify administrative actions to critical systems before allowing them to execute or be produced. Pre-production testing An important, often-overlooked step is to monitor implementation and perform pre-production testing to make sure your key controls work correctly. Some potential tests would be: Enter fake PHI, SSNs, account numbers or whatever data is appropriate to your environment to make sure those data types are being flagged or blocked. Test authentication and authorization by logging in and confirming what tools you can see and access. Test inbound and outbound network filtering to confirm only approved systems are reachable. Confirm the server(s) have been hardened according to the hardening policy. Confirm all critical events and actions are being logged. You’ve tried to work with the CTO and get him to agree to all these controls being implemented, but you don’t see the project plan changing or you’re getting fuzzy dates back. You may need to enlist other executives to help influence the decision. The risk management approach If you have a Risk Committee in place, it could help prioritize control requirements and timelines, so they’re implemented sooner rather than later. You need to be open to prioritizing certain controls over others to avoid major roadblocks and delays in moving the product forward. A proper AI Risk Assessment will help determine the applicable threats and controls to your environment, as well as the inherent and residual risks. For an AI threat list to build your risk assessment, I use the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications for my assessments and reporting. Scope the threats and rate their inherent risk in your environment. For a first pass, to speed up the assessment, you can drop threats with very low or low likelihood. For the Risk Committee, however, communicate the impacts in their language to help them understand. I would communicate the issues in terms of productivity loss, downtime, loss of customer trust, regulatory fines and other industry-specific impacts, such as patient care, trading errors, bad credit decisions, unfair claims or underwriting, worker safety and service availability. Don’t make it a quantitative exercise; keep it qualitative but be prepared to explain your ratings to maintain your peers’ trust. Good outcomes At this point, if all went well, you have provided the governance and input to limit risk to the organization. Incidents can and will cause downtime, fines and reputational damage if key controls are not in place. Helping your organization lower the risk of this occurring is a job well done.
summary: Your company’s CTO has a plan to implement your company’s first LLM-based application. The board approved it, and now you’re finding out about it. It’s a typical story I hear all the time, and I’ve lived it myself. You’ve heard everything about models and LLMs, but now you see this new term all over the place: Model Context Protocol ( MCP ) servers —and the realization that you now need to make sure they are implemented securely.

title: PHP2Shell will persist in enterprise environments for years
raw_text: Two critical vulnerabilities were announced last week in PHP , the internet’s most widely used web application runtime, and they came with the familiar warning to patch immediately. But CISOs will have to deal with the long tail of these flaws for years due to widespread PHP integration into third-party products with patching cycles customers don’t control. NAS devices, firewalls, VPN gateways, printers, building management panels, industrial IoT devices, and human-machine interfaces (HMIs) inside operational technology (OT) networks have web panels powered by PHP runtimes that cannot be patched directly. And many of these runtimes have unsupported versions for which upstream patches are not available. Vulnerabilities in widely used technologies can linger for years, and some deployments never get patched because they sit inside products that are out of support but still in service. One year after Log4Shell was disclosed in December 2021, nearly three quarters of organizations still had assets vulnerable to the critical flaw in the ubiquitous Log4j Java library, which remained a top attack vector in real-world attacks throughout 2023. PHP2Shell ( CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 ) could be even worse than Log4Shell for enterprises that cannot identify and patch all their assets — and attacks are already under way. On Monday, CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog , confirming active exploitation. Researchers had previously reported widespread scanning and attempted exploitation , but no confirmed compromise of production systems. “PHP2Shell has the potential to become a Log4Shell-scale event, but for a different reason,” Sai Molige, senior manager of threat hunting at Forescout, told CSO via email. “With Log4j, the main problem was finding a library you didn’t know you had. With PHP, much of the forgotten infrastructure will be found, but won’t have an upstream fix.” When patches for third-party appliances and software products can take weeks to arrive from vendors, security teams must reduce exposure by other means, both at the internet edge and inside internal networks. And that’s only after building an inventory of impacted assets, which is not straight forward for these flaws. The patching challenges The PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 as the official fixed versions, but relying on version numbers alone is not enough due to the way PHP is distributed. Most servers run Linux distributions that deliver application updates through their own package managers, including long-term support (LTS) distributions that bundle older PHP versions. In many cases, patches will have to be manually backported by package maintainers for those specific distros. For example, PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are officially end-of-life, even though they’re still widely used. The PHP developers published minimal source backports for those versions to help package maintainers, but PHP 7.3 and older were not covered at all. Vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck found that 42% of the 2.6 million internet-facing PHP hosts it scanned were running end-of-life branches, including 27% on PHP 3.x through 7.3 and 15% on 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1. Obtaining the fix on LTS distributions requires different approaches depending on the bundled PHP version. On Ubuntu 22.04 it arrives as a free PHP 8.1 update; on Ubuntu 20.04 the PHP 7.4 fix requires a Pro subscription; on Debian 11 the fix for the bundled PHP 7.4 sits behind a Freexian extended-support contract; and on AlmaLinux 8 it arrives as a backport for the retired PHP 7.2, 7.3, and 8.0. Red Hat Enterprise Linux, SUSE, Alpine, and Amazon Linux each draw their own support boundaries and those determine whether a fix exists at all for different distro versions. The version numbers for backported patches can also be inconsistent with upstream versions, adding to the inventory challenges. For example, AlmaLinux’s patched php-8.3.33-1.el10_2.alma.1 is below the upstream’s fixed version number for that branch: 8.3.36. Therefore, a scanner that reads a PHP version banner could flag a host as vulnerable even when the distribution has applied the fix. On top of all that, there are pre-built container, virtual machine, and firmware images for all sorts of third-party enterprise products that have their own bundled runtimes and that are much harder to inspect using automated scanners. “The PHP team has done a good job in a horrible situation,” said Eylam Milner, co-founder and CTO at software supply chain security firm Echo. “The problem for most companies is they don’t know where they’re running PHP. It’s in base images and in components that bundle their own runtime, and a lot of it is on versions older than 8.2 that are past end of life.” There are no public estimates on how many enterprise appliances or IoT and OT devices might run vulnerable versions of PHP, but they exist and some are reachable from the internet. Security firm Flare used internet scans from multiple sources that covered 2,220,231 service records from PHP hosts across 224 countries. In a regional sample across a single US state they identified NAS devices, VPN gateways, remote access portals, building automation systems, and physical access controllers . “Organizations still view PHP as a basic application dependency, but it’s often embedded deep inside appliances, hosting platforms, and upstream container images where day-one patching simply isn’t an option,” said Tom Kellermann, vice president of AI security and threat research at TrendAI. “The real battle isn’t just the vulnerability; it’s visibility.” PHP is also found inside industrial devices that can be in use for a decade or more and for which firmware patches take time to develop and deploy. Some of these devices need to be isolated until fixes arrive. Vulnerability management firm Cogent Security scanned dozens of Fortune 500 customer environments on the PHP2Shell disclosure day and found 2,266 affected assets per company on average , with 926 that were running the PHP service actively and 122 that were exposed to the internet. The company’s assessment focused on servers and virtual machines, not hardware appliances and OT devices. This highlights that the problem for enterprises won’t be the unavailability of scanners, but their lack of visibility inside all types of assets. As such, organizations will need a combination of strategies to discover all PHP installations in their environments: from versions reported by host-based package managers to network scanners and software bills of materials where available. Reducing exposure while waiting for patches Having an up-to-date inventory is important, but a complete map of PHP installations does not solve the issue of runtimes bundled in third-party products, each with its own patching schedule and mitigation instructions that can range from disabling the web management interface to completely isolating the device on the network. Just to give a few examples, Palo Alto Networks scheduled updates for some of its PAN-OS devices for this week and Siemens advised customers of its RUGGEDCOM APE1808 devices for industrial networks that are also powered by PAN-OS to follow Palo Alto’s advisory. Delta Controls patched its enterprise building management platform enteliWEB , but affected HVAC and room controllers are still awaiting firmware patches. Some NetModule IIoT and industrial routers from Belden are confirmed to be vulnerable but patches are still being developed. Until patches become available, which could take weeks in some cases, organizations will have to monitor the advisories for the third-party products they use and follow the temporary mitigations instructions for each of them. There will also likely be situations where some products have reached end of life and will never receive a patch, especially those supporting legacy applications organizations still need to keep operational. For a system that cannot be updated, the measures fall into three groups: Take the vulnerable web application off insecure network segments Put firewall controls in front of it Assess if a compromise may have already happened In some cases, management over HTTP or HTTPS might not be needed and the same functionality could be achieved over SSH or other protocols. For example, both Belden and Delta advise customers to disable the embedded HTTP server until patches become available. NetScaler advises customers to keep the management GUI and API reachable only from trusted administrative networks. As far as firewall detection rules go, there are some limitations. At the application layer, Web application firewalls (WAFs) can help, but they cannot block all PHP2Shell exploits that abuse multipart data uploads because they don’t usually inspect the full body of a web request, unlike the PHP engine. A WAF can scan for known attack patterns, but it doesn’t parse the internal structure of these form uploads deeply enough to catch all possible variations, so attackers can tweak the request formatting to potentially slip past the rules. For example, if a WAF looks only at the first few kilobytes of a request, an attacker can simply pad the beginning of their payload with junk data to push the malicious exploit code past the inspection limit. Furthermore, if an attacker manages to find the direct IP address of a backend system, they could completely bypass the WAF controls. That doesn’t mean that WAF rules are useless, but they are not a silver bullet against exploits. On the cloud side, AWS , Cloudflare , and Microsoft Azure offer WAF protection rules for PHP2Shell already and there are many local enterprise WAFs that have added detection as well. The other type of firewall protection is at the network layer via intrusion prevention systems (IPS). The issue with these firewalls is that they could be bypassed if they’re not configured to decrypt HTTPS traffic. IPS vendors have already created detections: Palo Alto has Threat ID 543004; Check Point has IPS protection CPAI-2026-15172; Cisco Talos has Snort rules 67359 and 67360 and Suricata rules 3000650 to 3000652 are also available. But deploying patches and alternative mitigations does not help systems that have already been compromised. And the longer it takes to implement these measures the more likely it is that attackers might have compromised a server. “The PHP2Shell flaws went from scanning noise to confirmed remote code execution on a honeypot within days of the October 21 patches, and that gap is where most real damage happens,” said Steve Povolny, vice president of AI strategy and security research at Exabeam. “Plenty of sites weren’t patched on day one. Some of those servers were probably exploited before anyone noticed, and installing the fix now does nothing about an intruder who got in last week. Patching closes the door. It doesn’t tell you who is already inside.” Any detection and prevention effort should be accompanied by an investigation of existing logs including web server access and error logs, PHP-FPM logs, WAF and reverse-proxy logs, CDN logs, EDR and process telemetry, DNS and egress logs, authentication logs, file-integrity monitoring, and cloud audit logs. How to know if you’ve already been hacked Things to look for in those logs are PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and a PHPSESSID cookie, multipart/form-data sent to endpoints that do not accept uploads, unusually large or malformed multipart bodies, deeply nested field names, repeated POSTs from one source, and spikes in HTTP 500 errors. Admins should also look for PHP-FPM, Apache, or httpd worker processes spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, base64, or various code interpreters, unexpected child processes under the web service account, reverse shells, outbound connections from web workers, as well as new or modified .php files in web root directories, upload directories and plugin directories. Abnormal PHPSESSID cookie length or corruption, unusually large session files, and unexplained worker restarts or segmentation faults could also be signs of exploitation, according to researchers from security firm Xint.io .
summary: Two critical vulnerabilities were announced last week in PHP , the internet’s most widely used web application runtime, and they came with the familiar warning to patch immediately. But CISOs will have to deal with the long tail of these flaws for years due to widespread PHP integration into third-party products with patching cycles customers don’t control. NAS devices, firewalls, VPN gateways, printers, building management panels, industrial IoT devices, and human-machine interfaces (HMIs) inside operational technology (OT) networks have web panels powered by PHP runtimes that cannot be patched directly. And many of these runtimes have unsupported versions for which upstream patches are not available.

title: Datacentre grid priority confirmed as connection queue response published
raw_text:
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has confirmed it will prioritise strategic demand and strategically align datacentre connections to the grid. That came on 28 October in its response to a consultation that drew 156 responses from across the industry.

The response completes a consultation that ran from 11 March to 15 April using powers taken under the Planning and Infrastructure Act to manage demand-side connections. 

It follows reforms that have already deprioritised up to 300GW of battery and solar capacity from the connection queue, as demand for electricity heads towards more than doubling by 2050. The 156 responses spanned developers, industry bodies and trade associations, network operators, local and mayoral authorities, consultancies, investors and technology suppliers. The largest single group, 42, came from demand-side project developers.

The programme is built around three pillars – Curate, Connect and Plan. Ofgem leads Curate, around speculation and queue management, and Connect, on flexibility and connection choice. Meanwhile, the government leads Plan, covering prioritisation of strategic demand and strategic alignment of datacentre connections.

Support for prioritisation was broad but not unanimous. Among demand-side project developers, 81% backed the introduction of prioritisation mechanisms, and 80% of non-datacentre demand developers agreed, arguing that strategic importance helps direct scarce capacity to projects that deliver wider economic and societal outcomes.

A further 14% of respondents were neutral, their support conditional on clear, published criteria for what counts as strategic demand. Eight respondents – five of them private individuals – disagreed. Investors warned that confidence depends on credible, well-sequenced implementation, and that government priorities could change over time.

On queue management, there was widespread agreement that speculative and non-viable projects have crowded out deliverable ones. Respondents backed datacentre-specific financial commitments but preferred refundable deposits tied to delivery milestones over non-refundable fees, and cautioned against extending charges to small businesses and low-margin sectors without affordability checks.

Respondents also stressed the importance of whole-system coordination and argued that demand-side reform must align across transmission and distribution and coordinate with water, land and, in some cases, gas infrastructure, rather than shifting bottlenecks elsewhere.

On aligning datacentre connections with regional infrastructure targets, half of the 137 respondents to that question agreed, a third were neutral, and 13% disagreed. Proponents said alignment would improve coordination between the grid operator and government, reduce unnecessary reinforcement and lower curtailment.

The government said it will take forward capacity reallocation, reservation and in-batch acceleration using Planning and Infrastructure Act powers, in time for the next grid application window. Strategic alignment of datacentre connections will follow post-2030, tied to regional infrastructure targets. Auctions for demand capacity remain under consideration, but the government said it is not committing to that at this stage. 

Alongside the response, Ofgem is consulting on a datacentre commitment fee of between £237,500 and £712,500 per megawatt of contracted capacity – equivalent to 2.5% to 7.5% of average project capital expenditure – to deter speculative demand.

Flexibility measures, including alternative connection agreements and voluntary flexibility services, will continue through the Connect workstream, along with a possible last-resort mechanism to curtail demand in security-of-supply emergencies. The government will also work with the National Energy System Operator (NESO) to identify locations with spare capacity before 2030.

Taken together with the datacentre covenant and the draft National Policy Statement, the response completes a coordinated push during Budget week to clear the connection queue of speculation and steer scarce grid capacity towards the datacentres the government deems strategic. 

Read more about datacentres and the grid

  • Can Britain’s grid keep up with the datacentre boom? Mounting power demands and grid bottlenecks are reshaping the geography of the UK’s digital infrastructure, pushing developers to wherever they can connect fastest.
  • UK government drafts national policy statement for datacentres: The draft policy opens England's fast-track NSIP regime to schemes of 100MW and above, with a presumption of consent and consultation running to 8 January 2027.
summary:
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has confirmed it will prioritise strategic demand and strategically align datacentre connections to the grid. That came on 28 October in its response to a consultation that drew 156 responses from across the industry.

The response completes a consultation that ran from 11 March to 15 April using powers taken under the Planning and Infrastructure Act to manage demand-side connections. 

It follows reforms that have already deprioritised up to 300GW of battery and solar capacity from the connection queue, as demand for electricity heads towards more than doubling by 2050. The largest single group, 42, came from demand-side project developers.

title: UK surveillance watchdog ‘disappointed’ over government investigatory powers failings
raw_text:
The UK investigatory powers commissioner has raised concerns over failures by some government agencies to follow safeguards in their use of surveillance and covert powers.

Brian Leveson said he was “disappointed and concerned” that a number of government bodies had failed to comply with safeguards under the Investigatory Powers Act, which governs surveillance and covert powers.

The commissioner said that overall, oversight was working well, but highlighted failures by the signals intelligence agency GCHQ, the National Crime Agency, the Prison Service and the Ministry of Defence in an annual report today.

MI5 lied to courts over Agent X

Leveson’s comments came after an investigation by the oversight body revealed that MI5 had lied to the courts and had misled the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office (IPCO) over its handling of Agent X, a violent neo-Nazi informer.

The former senior judge said today that the case of Agent X was “as serious as anything I have dealt with as commissioner”. MI5 had given false evidence to the High Court and the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, he said.

The failings identified in Leveson’s 2025 annual report raise wider questions about whether parts of the investigatory powers framework, particularly under the older Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, “remain clear, coherent and fit for purpose”.

“None of these are minor administrative failures,” he said. “Operational pressures are real, but they do not reduce the need for lawful, consistent and well-understood safeguards,” he added.

GCHQ’s lost devices

The investigatory powers commissioner criticised the signals intelligence agency GCHQ for failing to account for thousands of missing portable media devices that might contain secret data.

The agency had failed to explain what had happened to removable media years after being asked to do so by the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office.

The missing items include USB sticks, external hard drives, memory cards and other portable media storage devices used in GCHQ’s work.

GCHQ introduced a tool this year to monitor the issue, storage and location of removable media.

“We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate,” the IPCO report stated.

IPCO said His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service (HMPSS) was “continuing to get the basics wrong” when intercepting prisoners’ communications, with inspectors finding “recurring compliance issues”.

In one case, a prison wrongly intercepted calls between an inmate and their solicitor, causing significant “prejudice or harm” after misidentifying the phone number as the number of a social contact, though in that case the call was not listened to.

NCA handling of sources fell short

Leveson found that the National Crime Agency’s handling of covert human intelligence sources fell “well short of what the law requires and what I expect”.

Inspectors found “systematic weaknesses in governance and oversight” over the agency’s records of covert human intelligence sources and undercover work, held on computer systems and in manual files.

Significant volumes of records were held beyond their scheduled review dates, and material could not always reliably be linked to specific failures or subjects of interest, raising questions about the lawfulness of continued retention of records.

Police Service of Northern Ireland

The commissioner’s report also identified problems in the Police Service of Northern Ireland’s (PSNI) handling of confidential and sensitive material.

The PSNI failed to inform IPCO inspectors of a surveillance operation against Belfast journalists Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney during an annual inspection, breaching the PSNI’s statutory duty of candour to IPCO inspectors, as previously reported by Computer Weekly.     

The police force also failed to alert IPCO inspectors to a covert surveillance operation against investigative journalist Dónal MacIntyre, which sought to covertly monitor his social media posts.

Leveson disclosed that IPCO had carried out an interim inspection of the PSNI in December 2025.

Inspectors agreed with the findings of the McCullough Review that there was no evidence of the PNSI’s anti-corruption unit using a standalone system to bypass the authorisation process for monitoring journalists’ phone records.

“We are considering carefully whether the review’s findings have any wider application, particularly in relation to levels of understanding, legal advice and training on confidential material across the law enforcement community,” the report stated.

The report also highlighted that the Ministry of Defence had failed to properly apply safeguards to protect people detained overseas, who may be interrogated or interviewed to gather intelligence which is passed to the UK.

Schedule 7 stops

Other parts of the report revealed that GCHQ wrongly identified several people as suspects in terrorism-related activity, following an “issue” with an undisclosed software application they were using.

Errors in communications data linked to one mobile phone operator led to 72 false positives and 88 false negatives in the identification of IP addresses. As a result, two innocent people were arrested.

A timing mistake by a telecommunications operator led to the police arresting the wrong person during an investigation to identify a caller who had threatened significant harm to local people.

In another historical case, it emerged that an innocent person had been arrested and detained for questioning and that three generations of the same family were mistakenly visited at separate addresses and questioned.

In both cases, police officers had failed to heed warnings from the telecommunications operator over the reliability of its data.

Leveson said that demands on IPCO were increasing and that he was exploring how new technologies and automation could support the organisation.

Despite raising serious concerns, Leveson said his assessment was that independent oversight is working.

“I remain satisfied that, across a demanding and fast-changing environment, the system of checks on the use of covert powers continues to operate with rigour and independence,” he said.

IPCO provides independent oversight of the use of investigatory powers by intelligence agencies, police forces and other public authorities, under the Investigatory Powers Act. It has a remit of 600 bodies.

title: Datacentre covenant pleases developers more than campaigners
raw_text:
Chancellor John Healey’s announcement of a datacentre covenant drew fire from campaigners and industry alike after Wednesday’s Autumn Budget. Critics branded the centrepiece of the government’s AI infrastructure push a voluntary smokescreen that binds big tech to nothing.

The covenant, published by HM Treasury on 28 October, made priority grid connections and, where necessary, permission to build on-site generation conditional on strict tests around local investment, jobs, water and the environment. Strategic datacentres will be expected to agree a Local Benefit Plan, protect water supplies, capture waste heat and pay their fair share of energy costs in return for a faster route to power.

The covenant lists five tests. Datacentres should:

  • Pay their fair share of energy costs so households and businesses do not pick up the bill.
  • Invest in improving local communities.
  • Adhere to the highest environmental standards.
  • Create jobs, apprenticeships and reindustrialisation.
  • Strengthen Britain’s security. 

The grid measures are reserved for strategic datacentres, whose definition is still to come.

Healey framed the offer around sovereignty, arguing that when the NHS uses artificial intelligence (AI) to treat patients, or the armed forces use it to keep the country safe, that data should stay in Britain. 

The government estimates the UK needs 6GW of AI-capable datacentre capacity by 2030 and casts the covenant as a clear offer – faster delivery of the datacentres the country needs in exchange for responsible development. Measures include reserving and reallocating grid capacity for strategic projects, and a tightly controlled framework that permits on-site generation only for exceptionally strategic sites.

The covenant and a draft National Policy Statement (NPS), published the same day, are two parts of the same strategy. The covenant sets out the five tests datacentres should meet, and that strategic datacentres must meet to qualify for faster grid connections and on-site generation. The NPS, from the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, turns those tests into assessment criteria the Planning Inspectorate and the Secretary of State will apply when deciding development consent for schemes of 100MW and above. 

Campaigners unconvinced by covenant

John Ridd, co-founder and chief executive of Greenpixie, said the covenant was “a smokescreen designed to appease local resistance to AI infrastructure”, adding that the requirements Healey claimed were new “already exist, but Big Tech is never held accountable”. He said the average datacentre “employs fewer people than a local supermarket” and urged the government to increase capacity through efficiency, “not just be railroaded into building more datacentres”.

Oliver Hayes, head of campaigns at Global Action Plan, said the chancellor “is in for a shock” if he thinks communities “will be hoodwinked by a voluntary ‘covenant’ that could have been written by Big Tech themselves and explicitly allows for power generation from heavily polluting on-site fossil fuels”. He added: “Voluntarism doesn’t work with these companies.” 

Foxglove head of communications Tom Hegarty said there “does not appear to be a single legally binding environmental commitment” in the document. He described it as “voluntary at best for Big Tech” while strategic datacentres would be handed “a golden ticket to skip the grid connection queue”. He said the charity would keep challenging datacentres in court.

One campaigner at the sharp end – currently battling a Wiltshire County Council decision to grant consent to the Spring Park datacentre being developed by Ark Data Centres – felt the covenant’s provisions may make little difference.

Morgyn Davies of the Neston & Westwells Action Group (NWAG) said: “When legal agreements between developers and councils are signed in secret, behind closed doors, something much tougher than a ‘voluntary covenant’ is needed to guarantee communities do not suffer a catastrophic tomorrow so the developer can make a massive profit today.”

Industry voices welcoming but uneasy

James Hart, chief executive of BCS Consultancy, said the covenant was “a welcome recognition of the strategic importance of digital infrastructure” but “the deal is lopsided, with clear obligations for developers but less certainty around what government can deliver in return”. 

“A covenant doesn’t build substations,” he added. Chris Coward, BCS’s chief operating officer, warned that continued grid uncertainty “pushes developers towards alternative power solutions, particularly on-site gas generation”.

Rich Kenny, managing director of datacentre efficiency specialist Interact and chair of the IEEE Water Resource Technologies Working Group, said the covenant was “a move in the right direction so long as it has enough teeth to ensure those local benefits are delivered when promised”.

Datacentre builders welcome elements 

Giles Hanglin, chief executive of UK-based clean energy and datacentre developer Apatura Energy, said the proposed Ministerial Control Centre and its powers to reserve and reallocate connections was “the strongest measure set out” in yesterday’s Budget, but warned that “if that takes months, the fast lane will not be fast”.

Matthew Baynes, vice-president of secure power and datacentres for equipment supplier Schneider Electric in the UK and Ireland, said the commitment to prioritising grid connections for critical datacentres was “particularly encouraging”.

The covenant lands weeks after MSPs in Scotland voted to pause planning decisions on large datacentres until national guidance arrives. Scotland’s committed pipeline has grown to 14 schemes and 2.4GW, the fastest growth of any UK region, while the grid connection queue, rather than planning consent, remains the binding constraint on much of the UK pipeline. Ireland shows what happens when development outruns the grid.

Read more about datacentres and planning

  • Data dive – government 2030 datacentre capacity targets look shaky: We analyse why DSIT’s 6GW AI-capable capacity target for 2030 is out of reach unless operators accelerate delivery.

title: UK government drafts national policy statement for datacentres
raw_text:
The government has published the first draft of its National Policy Statement (NPS) for datacentres. It plans to open England’s Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) regime to datacentre schemes of 100MW and above and instruct the secretary of state to begin from a presumption of consent.

The 94-page draft, from the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), sets the framework the Planning Inspectorate and Secretary of State will use to decide applications for development consent for large datacentres.

It adopts the five tests set out in the Data Centre Covenant, published the same day, as its assessment criteria. 

Publication of the statement came alongside a call for views on the NPS that closes at 11.59pm on 8 January 2027.

The document sets an indicative minimum of 100MW of rated IT load capacity for a project to be directed into the NSIP regime, a threshold it argues reserves the route for only the largest and most nationally significant sites.

Projects below it would continue to pass through the Town and Country Planning Act.

The statement must complete its parliamentary stages before it is designated and takes effect. Once designated, the Planning Inspectorate would examine applications for the secretary of state to decide them against its published criteria rather than through case-by-case judgement.

The NPS sits in a wider policy stack that includes:

  • Designation of the sector as critical national infrastructure;
  • Five AI Growth Zones;
  • A Ministerial Control Centre for the most strategic projects;
  • Planning reform through the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 and the National Planning Policy Framework published in August 2026.

The NPS grounds its case in sovereignty, arguing that as AI and data become central to healthcare, defence and public services, Britain cannot depend on infrastructure located overseas. It cites £19.4bn of foreign direct investment in UK datacentres since July 2024, an estimated estate of more than 220 datacentres with about 2GW of capacity, and 73GW across roughly 315 projects sitting in the grid connection queue.

It points to the government’s Compute Roadmap forecast that the UK needs at least 6GW of AI-capable datacentre capacity by 2030 – about three times current capacity – and an increase in datacentre planning applications of more than 60% in 2025. Global demand projections by Goldman Sachs cited in the report suggest the market could grow by up to 165% by 2030.

The statement also argues that not all UK datacentre needs can be met by overseas infrastructure. Sensitive government, health and financial data must be processed under UK regulatory and security frameworks, it says, adding that latency-sensitive sectors such as finance and university research depend on nearby capacity rather than remote compute.

The presumption of consent means a development consent order is unlikely to be refused where a scheme meets the NPS requirements, applies the mitigation hierarchy and satisfies legal requirements. Exceptions include unmitigable harm to habitat sites, unacceptable risk to human health or defence, and sites in the Green Belt.

Read more about datacentres and planning

  • UK committed datacentre pipeline grows to more than 14GW: Barbour ABI data show UK’s datacentre pipeline has grown to 173 projects and more than 14GW of capacity, driven by AI demand and large sites in Scotland and the North East.
  • Can Britain’s grid keep up with the datacentre boom? Mounting power demands and grid bottlenecks are reshaping the geography of the UK’s digital infrastructure, pushing developers to wherever they can connect fastest.

The document stresses that the presumption does not create a new need case or extra weighting. It applies only after normal consideration of the need case and satisfaction of the NPS and legal requirements, and applications must still satisfy the Habitats Regulations, including consideration of alternatives and compensatory measures.

Applicants must still submit an Environmental Impact Assessment and a Habitats Regulations Assessment, and provide evidence on biodiversity net gain, water and grid connections. The assessment principles also cover climate change mitigation and adaptation, environmental regulation, safety and security. The NPS expects datacentres to capture waste heat “wherever practical”, minimise water use, and publish annual energy and water data. It defines the scope of facilities it covers, distinguishing them from other digital infrastructure such as cloud services.

The government published an Appraisal of Sustainability and a Habitats Regulations Assessment alongside the draft. The NPS applies to England only, and may be a material consideration for decisions in Scotland and Wales. It arrives weeks after MSPs voted to pause planning decisions on large Scottish datacentres until national guidance appears.

The Chancellor introduced the datacentre covenant in the Autumn Budget, alongside the government’s response to its grid connections consultation. It forms one part of a three-part push to make the planning and power system deliver datacentres faster.

title: Having a PHP patch available does not mean you're protected
raw_text:
The critical PHP vulnerabilities disclosed earlier in October are a stark reminder that a single flaw can trigger a global domino effect across borders and industries within hours, leaving organisations worldwide exposed to the same threat at once.

Having a security patch available is essential. However, a patch is not a silver bullet solution. Turning patches into effective protection demands qualified professionals, clear responsibilities and the operational readiness to act.

You can’t protect what you don’t know

On 21 October, when European authorities issued a joint warning about two PHP vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely on vulnerable servers without authentication, another issue was highlighted.

While security updates have since been released, organisations were forced to confront the fact that they hadn’t even realised which products and services depend on PHP. Authorities have urged businesses to identify affected applications, coordinate with providers and prioritise internet-facing systems. But unfortunately, cyber resilience isn’t something organisations can switch on when a crisis hits.

For many businesses, their greatest vulnerability may be a dependency they do not know exists. As we’ve recently seen, a company can have robust internal security procedures and still be exposed through a supplier, an application or a component buried several layers into its technology infrastructure. The challenge is no longer simply protecting the systems an organisation owns but also understanding the systems it depends on across its entire supply chain.

From an alert to an accountable response

For business leaders, the immediate question is whether their organisation can establish its exposure and demonstrate that it has addressed risk across its entire supply chain. A company may receive assurances that its external provider has updated a customer portal but have they checked whether the company’s other applications rely on the same vulnerable components?

Vulnerability management is a critical role in any business, and it needs clear ownership. Patching fast when vulnerabilities are identified is a challenge, especially as AI is increasing the pace of such identification. Technical teams must implement and test corrections in relation to the application and local architectural context for ensuring smooth operation after patching. Security managers must assess priorities, coordinate  resources and communicate the implications for the business. Auditors must independently evaluate whether the controls supporting that response are adequate and operating effectively.

While these roles are critical, increased demand for security oversight is further weighing down stretched cybersecurity teams. In September, ISACA's State of Cybersecurity 2026 research found that 56% of European respondents report that their organisations' cyber security teams are understaffed, while 55% say they are underfunded. These constraints can make it harder to investigate exposure, coordinate remediation and verify that security fixes have been implemented effectively.

In an environment that only gets more complex, cyber security professionals are expected to do more work, faster, and with small teams. Increased investment is non-negotiable if organisations want even basic cyber security.

Read more PHP2Shell coverage

  • What to do as critical PHP flaws put millions of websites at risk.
  • PHP2Shell: 22M exposed servers at risk as emergency patches released.
  • Critical PHP vulnerabilities expose most websites to potential compromise. (Cybersecurity Dive)
  • PHP2Shell bugs signal red alert for security industry. (Dark Reading)
  • PHP2Shell disclosure unravels after leaks forced early patch drop.
  • Botched PHP2Shell disclosure revealed as panic continues.
  • PHP exploitation moves at slower-than-expected pace, but millions remain at risk (Cybersecurity Dive)
  • Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber experts weigh in with advice (Dark Reading)
  • EU makes progress towards PHP patching, UK lags.
  • Cisa, security researchers confirm successful exploitation of PHP flaws (Cybersecurity Dive).
  • PHP2Shell: US updates Kev catalogue as exploits spread.
  • PHP2Shell explained: Timeline of the global vulnerability crisis.
  • Wave of PHP2Shell-style flaws coming, Nvidia security exec predicts.
  • Insurance industry fears potential impacts from PHP2Shell. (Cybersecurity Dive)

    Building resilience before the next alert

    Cyber resilience must be built before a crisis hits. An accurate inventory of assets and dependencies, established supplier contacts and procedures for urgent changes give teams a foundation for action. They also need to know how to verify remediation and manage disruption if a service must be temporarily isolated.

    Business leaders should determine whether those capabilities receive sufficient investment. They must ensure that teams have the resources, skills and authority to monitor for vulnerabilities and act when needed. Unsupported systems must receive attention and processes must be introduced so that significant risks reach the people empowered to address them. Preparedness should be tested through exercises and reviewed after real incidents.

    Investment must also extend to the next generation of cybersecurity professionals. As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, defenders need the skills to use it responsibly to identify weaknesses, assess findings and support remediation. Continuous learning, technical experience and professional judgement will be essential to translating that speed into better protection.

    Technology will never be completely free of vulnerabilities. The real test is whether organisations have the governance, expertise and operational readiness to prevent a software flaw from becoming a wider business crisis. In an interconnected economy, the quality of that preparation has consequences far beyond any single company.

    Chris Dimitriadis is global chief strategy officer at ISACA

title: Controversial Fujitsu contract extension on the cards at Post Office
raw_text:
Fujitsu is set to see its relationship with the Post Office extended further as it takes longer than anticipated to unwrap the controversial 30-year relationship.

Slower-than-expected progress transitioning from Fujitsu has cast doubt on whether the supplier’s contract end date, when Accenture was due to take over the running of Horizon, will be met.

Fujitsu’s current contract with the Post Office will expire in March 2027, but there was an option to extend written into the last agreement that, due to slower than expected progress, looks more likely to be taken up.

In November 2025, the deal was extended 12 months to March 2027, costing an additional £41m, which was criticised by Post Office scandal victims and campaigners.

Another extension was always possible, with that tender including an option for up to another 12 months, which sources now believe will inevitably be taken up. The tender said: “… Based on the transition plan from replacement supplier, further extension of 6-12 months may be required.”

According to sources, things are also progressing slower than expected on the transfer away from Fujitsu. Even if just for months, an extension to Fujitsu’s relationship with the Post Office, which began in the mid-1990s when it took over ICL, would mean millions more pounds being paid to Fujitsu. 

There was also a delay in signing the contract for the software that will replace Horizon. As revealed by Computer Weekly, the signing of the Post Office’s contract with OneView Commerce, a cloud-based electronic point of sale (EPOS) software supplier, was delayed six times and for nearly three months due to a legal dispute with the losing bidder, Escher. The contract was initially set to be formally signed on 3 June, but was not signed off until 24 August. 

Read more about NBIT

  • Post Office set to axe in-house-developed New Branch IT software.
  • Post Office IT transformation project was ‘set up to fail’, chairman tells inquiry.
  • Post Office spending £80,000+ a week on engineers who can’t work, as IT project burns cash.
  • Fujitsu set for further £180m deal as Post Office Horizon replacement delayed.
  • Post Office Horizon replacement project labelled ‘unachievable’ as taxpayer bill reaches £1bn.

A Post Office spokesperson said: “The Post Office signed a contract with Accenture in June to take on the day-to-day running of Horizon from Fujitsu. Work to transition the existing Horizon system over to Accenture is continuing collaboratively and at pace. In addition, working with our partners, our plans relating to what our new system would entail and how it could be rolled out across the network are ahead of schedule at present. The Post Office has previously stated to Computer Weekly that ‘Fujitsu will be completely removed from its Post Office contract by the summer of 2027’. That remains our position.”

The Horizon replacement project was first planned almost exactly seven years ago, after the Post Office admitted defeat in the Alan Bates and Others versus Post Office group litigation, when it was proved Horizon errors caused the account shortfalls that subpostmasters were blamed and punished for. But nothing really moved, and it was only after the ITV dramatisation of the Post Office scandal in January 2024, amid public outrage, that things started to happen.

This culminated in the £1.8bn New Branch IT (NBIT) project, but this ran into trouble and was eventually axed in May 2024, and was replaced by the current project, which sees an off-the-shelf EPOS system replace Horizon in a £169.2m contract with OneView Commerce, with Accenture providing outsourcing services through a £322.8m contract.

There have been multiple Fujitsu extensions worth nearly £200m since 2019.

Meaningless apologies

With the Post Office scandal public inquiry’s final conclusions expected early next year, the timing of an extention could also be highly controversial. Fujitsu is expected to be heavily criticized in the report, which will examine the causes of the scandal in detail.

An initial inquiry report that looked at the human impact of the scandal, which was covered in Phase 1, found among many disturbing impacts that it could not be ruled out that 13 suicides were caused by the scandal.

Despite its repeated apologies, Fujitsu has done little to convince victims of its regret and intention to make amends.

Following the publication of the inquiry’s first report, in summer 2025, Computer Weekly revealed that a senior Fujitsu executive told staff in a meeting that the report was “not that bad”.

His recorded remarks about the devastating inquiry findings are at odds with Fujitsu’s apologetic statements. In stark contrast the report, which was published in July 2025, they were described as “profoundly disturbing” by the Post Office Horizon scandal public inquiry chair, Wyn Williams.

Furthermore, in April 2024, just after the scandal and Fujitsu’s role in it became wide public knowledge, the supplier promised, as a gesture, not to bid for government contracts. But through leaked comms, Computer Weekly revealed how the supplier’s staff were instructed how to bid for government contracts during the self-imposed ban.

Adding to the frustration and anger of victims, the supplier has repeatedly refused to commit to an amount it will pay towards the billions of pounds in costs associated with a scandal it was partly to blame for, waiting for the publication of the inquiry report.

Read more: Fujitsu’s role in the Post Office scandal: Everything you need to know

Almost immediately after the ITV drama about the scandal made it headline news, opening it up to the wider public, the then Fujitsu European boss said the supplier had a “moral obligation” to pay towards the costs of the scandal.

But an extention to the contract could see millions of pounds of taxpayer money heading Fujitsu’s way before the supplier pays a penny towards the cost of the scandal.

If an extension is required, it could come around the time of the main public inquiry report. This will look at phases 2 to 7 of the public inquiry, which will include forensic examination of the part Fujitsu and its staff played in what is often referred to as the widest miscarriage of justice in British history.

Nothing surprises us

Former subpostmaster Scott Darlington, who had his wrongful conviction for false accounting overturned in 2021, said nothing shocks him anymore when it comes to the scandal.

“There are so many things that are hard to believe, this is just another one to pile on top,” he said.

Pete Murray, a former subpostmaster based in Northwest England, who lost his business and had his life shattered as a result of the Post Office scandal, said: “There is no surprise if the contract gets extended. It’s just the same old story.”

Former subpostmaster Jo Hamilton, who had a wrongful conviction for false accounting overturned alongside Darlington, agreed that nothing comes as a surprise after years fighting the Post Office. “The whole thing is just a mess, but we are used to it, so no surprises,” she said.
